questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-week history of an increasingly large and painful lump on his right shoulder. The lump began as a pea-sized red bump. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F); all other vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a 5-cm, inflamed carbuncle on the right shoulder. Treatment with a 7-day course of cephalexin is initiated. The carbuncle in this patient is most likely located in the layer of skin that has which of the following embryologic precursors?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Embryologically, a dermatome describes the primordial tissue that gives rise to the dermis, which in the developed form includes nerves, blood vessels, connective tissue, sweat glands, and hair follicles. A carbuncle describes a group of infected hair follicles, generally from the Staphylococcus species, and is commonly referred to as a “boil.” Infection within the dermis is therefore located in a layer of skin that began as an embryologic dermatome.

In the developed organism, a dermatome describes an area of skin supplied by a spinal nerve ganglion. Nerve fibers from the dermatome send afferent signals to the central nervous system which then responds with efferent signals causing the patient pain in the affected area.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

A myotome (Choice B) describes the muscles supplied by a spinal nerve root in the developed organism. In embryologic terms, a myotome is the primordial tissue that gives rise to a muscle or group of muscles. The myotome would not be affected by a superficial skin infection or abscess. Deep abscesses can extend through to involve muscle; however, there is no evidence of abscess in this case.

A neurotome (Choice C) or neuromere describes components of the neural tube that help establish the embryonic brain during development.

A sclerotome (Choice D) describes the part of the developing embryo giving rise to bones and musculoskeletal tissue.

A syndetome (Choice E) describes the component of the somite comprising tendon progenitor cells. These components would not be affected by a superficial skin infection.

Educational Objective: A dermatome refers to the embryologic precursor that gives rise to the dermis, and in the developed form, refers to the area of dermis innervated by a single spinal sensory nerve. Afferent fibers travel from the dermatome and provide sensory signals to the central nervous system, triggering an efferent response. This response may cause sensations including pain. Carbuncles, which are commonly caused by the Staphylococcus species, form within the dermis.

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with a 10-day history of a blistering rash on his back comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He completed a course of antiviral medication 3 days ago, and he continues to have moderate pain. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. This rash is most likely located in which of the following dermatomes?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

A dermatome describes an area of skin supplied by a spinal nerve ganglion. Nerve fibers from the dermatome send afferent signals to the central nervous system which responds with efferent signals causing pain in the affected area. The T11 dermatome travels in a band-like arc from the lower thoracic spine to the anterior abdomen, terminating just below the umbilicus. Herpes zoster, which is a reactivation of latent/dormant varicella virus, often affects thoracic dermatomes, though any dermatome can be affected. It initially presents as pain and paresthesia in a dermatomal pattern that progresses to a group of clustered vesicles on an erythematous base over several days. As the rash evolves, the vesicles rupture and become crusted. Following resolution of the infection, the skin changes also resolve. Patients may experience post-herpetic neuralgia and persistent pain at the site of reactivation, even after resolution of herpes zoster. Herpes zoster infection, when localized, generally affects only one dermatome because the virus replicates in the dorsal root ganglion of a single spinal nerve. Disseminated zoster infection across multiple dermatomes can occur in the setting of severe infection or immunocompromise. Herpes zoster is generally treated with antiviral medications, including acyclovir or valacyclovir, as well as medication for pain management.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

The T4 (Choice A) dermatome extends from the upper thoracic spine to the areola anteriorly. It is superior to the T11 dermatome.

The T7 (Choice B) dermatome extends from the mid thoracic spine to the skin between the areola and umbilicus. It is superior to the T11 dermatome.

The L1 (Choice D) dermatome extends from the upper lumbar spine to the inguinal area. It is inferior to the T11 dermatome.

The S1 (Choice E) dermatome extends from the upper sacrum down the lower extremities. It is inferior to the T11 dermatome.

Educational Objective: Herpes zoster infection presents in a dermatomal distribution and results from varicella virus reactivation in the dorsal root ganglion of a nerve. The T11 dermatome extends from the inferior thoracic spine to the inferior abdominal wall below the umbilicus.

questions.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of an itchy rash for 3 days. Physical examination shows an excoriated rash over the right wrist and around the waist. A 1.5-cm linear tunnel is seen over the right wrist. A photomicrograph of scrapings from the affected area is shown. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer:  D.

Sarcoptes scabiei is a mite that is transmissible by skin-to-skin contact, typically by family members or sexual partners. Skin infestation typically occurs on the sides or webs of the fingers, wrists, axillae, areolae, or genitalia, and leads to intense pruritus. Physical examination commonly shows several small, erythematous papules that are frequently excoriated from scratching and may reveal mite burrows. In some cases, lesions have a crusted appearance. Diagnosis of scabies is confirmed by microscopic examination showing mites, eggs, or feces. Scabies is managed with topical or oral antiparasitic agents, such as permethrin.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Leishmania donovani (Choice A) is a member of the protozoa genus Leishmania and is one of several species associated with development of leishmaniasis. Leishmaniasis has cutaneous and visceral forms. The vector for leishmaniasis is the sandfly. A pink papule with overlying crust may develop at the site of a bite on uncovered skin. Additional cutaneous lesions may develop and spread along the draining lymphatics. In leishmaniasis, histopathologic visualization of amastigotes within macrophages on blood smear or tissue biopsy is diagnostic.

Loa loa (Choice B) is a parasitic worm passed to humans from deerflies and is native to west and central Africa. Loiasis is caused by loa loa infection and presents with itchy, non-painful swellings commonly involving the skin surrounding joints, as well as the eyelids.

Malassezia furfur (Choice C) causes tinea versicolor, which clinically presents with hypopigmented and hyperpigmented macules and patches with a fine scale, and at sites of high sebum production, including the chest and back. A KOH preparation of a skin scraping is diagnostic and will show fungal spores and short hyphae along the edges of epidermal cells. Tinea versicolor may be treated using topical antifungal preparations, including topical ketoconazole or selenium sulfide preparations.

Trichophyton mentagrophytes (Choice E) is a dermatophyte that can cause superficial infection on any part of the skin, but most commonly affects the scalp (tinea capitis), trunk or extremities (tinea corporis), nail (tinea unguium), groin (tinea cruris), and foot (tinea pedis). This may be treated using topical antifungal preparations, including topical ketoconazole.

Educational Objective: Scabies is a skin infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, which is transmissible by skin-to-skin contact, typically by family members or sexual partners. Scabies occurs on the sides or webs of the fingers, wrists, axillae, areolae, or genitalia and is associated with intense pruritus. Physical examination commonly shows several small, erythematous papules that are frequently excoriated, and diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic examination of a skin scraping showing mites, eggs, or feces. Scabies is managed with topical or oral antiparasitic agents including permethrin.

questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of pain at the base of her right thumb. She does not recall any trauma but says that she typically carries her heavy 6-month-old son with her right arm. Her vital signs are within normal limits. A test involving flexion of the fingers over the thumb to make a fist, followed by ulnar deviation, is positive on the right. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's pain?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Tenosynovitis of the thumb, also termed de Quervain tenosynovitis, involves the first dorsal extensor compartment, which contains the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons. Overuse of these tendons causes inflammation of the compartment, leading to pain at the base of the thumb that can radiate up the thumb or forearm. Tenosynovitis refers to inflammation of tendon, tendon sheath, and associated synovial tissue. It is commonly seen in mothers who hold their babies with their thumb extended and abducted. Diagnosis is performed with the Finkelstein test, in which the patient grasps their thumb in a closed fist, and the provider deviates their wrist in an ulnar (medial) direction. Pain elicited along the base of the thumb or radial aspect of the wrist is suggestive of de Quervain tenosynovitis. Treatment is typically conservative and includes activity modification, NSAIDs, splinting, and steroid injection.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Bursitis (Choice A) is inflammation of the thin, sac-like, fluid-filled structures that reduce friction and permit motion between layers of connective tissue, generally between tendons, ligaments, and bones. It is more commonly associated with larger structures, such as the greater trochanter and olecranon, but rarely occurs in the hand. It presents with localized tenderness, swelling, erythema, and warmth, and can be diagnosed with ultrasonography or MRI.

Enthesitis (Choice B) is inflammation of the sites where tendons and ligaments insert into bone. It is associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies, such as psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. Because it commonly presents as part of a larger systemic inflammatory process, treatment includes NSAIDs and disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs.

Osteoarthritis (Choice C) of the carpal-metacarpal (CMC) joint of the thumb is more common in older patients. It presents with pain localized to the base of the thumb and difficulty with grasping and pinching motions. Pain elicited by a CMC grind test is suggestive of this diagnosis, which can be confirmed with evidence of osteoarthritis on x-ray.

Osteomyelitis (Choice D) is an infection of bone and bone marrow that occurs in acute, subacute, and chronic variants. Caused by direct inoculation or hematogenous spread of bacteria, patients typically present with localized pain and inflammation, low-grade fever, and increased inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein). MRI is the best modality for diagnosis, but x-rays can reveal localized erosion in subacute and chronic disease.

Educational Objective: De Quervain tenosynovitis of the thumb is classically seen in young mothers due to the repetitive strain caused by carrying infants. Tenosynovitis refers to inflammation of the tendon, tendon sheath, and associated synovial tissue. Diagnosis can be confirmed by a positive Finkelstein test. Treatment is typically conservative and includes activity modification, NSAIDs, splinting, and steroid injection.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-month history of an enlarging, painless lump on the back of his left thigh. He also has had weakness in his left thigh and leg. Physical examination shows a 7-cm, hard, nonmobile swelling on the left posterior thigh. Sensation to pinprick is decreased along the posterior thigh and below the knee. Sagittal and axial views from a CT scan of the left thigh are shown. A biopsy specimen of the lump confirms a rhabdomyosarcoma. The most likely cause of the findings in this patient is compression of which of the following nerves?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rare, aggressive neoplasm of mesenchymal skeletal muscle precursors that may occur in the orbit, head and neck, genitourinary tract, and musculoskeletal system. Histology shows small, round, blue cells that are desmin positive. Neoplasms of the lower extremities can compress peripheral nerves. the affected nerve can often be identified by the pattern of weakness and sensory loss. The sciatic nerve is a large nerve that originates from the lumbosacral plexus (L4 to S3) and travels down the posterior thigh to the popliteal fossa. Above the knee, it provides motor innervation to the posterior compartment (eg, hamstrings) and sensory innervation to the posterior thigh. The sciatic nerve splits into the common peroneal and tibial nerves at the popliteal fossa. These branches supply all muscles of the lower extremity below the knee and provide sensory innervation to the entire lower extremity below the knee except for the medial leg. Compression of the sciatic nerve presents with weakness of hip extension, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, eversion, and inversion, as well as impaired sensation in its territory.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

The femoral nerve (Choice A) arises from the lumbar plexus (L2 to L4). It innervates the anterior compartment of the thigh (eg, quadriceps muscles, sartorius) and provides sensation for the anterior thigh and anteromedial leg via the saphenous branch. Femoral nerve compression presents with weakness of hip flexion and knee extension, diminished patellar reflex, and impaired sensation of the anterior thigh.

The ilioinguinal nerve (Choice B) supplies sensation to the base of the penis and anterior scrotum and is also involved in the cremasteric reflex arc. It does not innervate the lower extremity.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (Choice C) originates from the lumbar plexus (L2 to L3) and supplies sensation to the lateral thigh. Impingement can cause impaired sensation and paresthesia in its territory.

The obturator nerve (Choice D) arises from the lumbar plexus (L2 to L4). It innervates the medial compartment of the thigh (eg, adductor muscles, gracilis muscle) and provides sensation for the medial thigh. Obturator nerve compression typically presents with impairment in hip adduction and sensation of the medial proximal thigh. Impaired sensation of the posterior thigh and distal lower extremity would be atypical.

The posterior cluneal nerves (Choice E) arise from the lumbosacral plexus and provide sensory innervation to the skin of the buttocks. Compression results in paresthesia and impaired sensation of the lower back and buttocks regions.

It innervates the hamstrings as well as all muscles below the knee and provides sensory innervation to the entire lower extremity below the knee except for the medial leg. Compression of the sciatic nerve presents with weakness of hip extension, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, eversion, and inversion, as well as impaired sensation in its territory.

questions.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician after his teacher reported that he has difficulty sprinting. He is able to exercise normally at a less vigorous pace. After exercise of the right upper extremity, a blood sample obtained from the vein just proximal to the exercised muscle does not show the expected increase in serum lactic acid concentration. An inborn error of metabolism in which of the following pathways in skeletal muscle is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Glycogen storage disease type V (McArdle disease) presents with fatigue and muscle cramping during exertion, typically in a patient who is otherwise developmentally normal. It is caused by an inborn defect in glycogenolysis, which is necessary to supply the active cell with substrate for making adenosine triphosphate. Free glucose is consumed rapidly during the initial phase of exercise, after which muscle switches to degradation of glycogen for metabolism. Glycogen storage disease type V is caused by a deficiency in skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase (also termed myophosphorylase deficiency), which hydrolyzes 1,4-glycosidic bonds to liberate glucose-1-phosphate monomers from glycogen molecules. Inability to break down glycogen results in muscle cramping, fatigue, and mild rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria. Resting creatine kinase concentrations may be mildly increased. Muscle breakdown can lead to electrolyte abnormalities and consequent arrhythmias. Blood glucose concentrations usually remain normal. Generally, after the initial fatigue and cramping, patients can resume exercising because muscle blood flow increases, and alternative forms of energy are utilized via gluconeogenesis and protein catabolism. The diagnosis is suspected on history and confirmed by genetic testing and biopsy showing increased muscle glycogen and potentially absent myophosphorylase. Alternatively, the diagnosis can be confirmed with an exertional forearm exercise test. When deprived of glucose, exercising muscle will break down protein and generate ammonia. The increased serum ammonia and absence of lactate indicates impaired glycolysis from the absence of glucose.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Beta oxidation (Choice A) is the process by which fatty acids are converted into ketones and citric acid cycle substrates. It is impaired in medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, a defect in the ability to convert fatty acids into acetyl CoA; this presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, liver dysfunction, vomiting, lethargy, and seizures, and can lead to sudden death.

Gluconeogenesis (Choice B) is impaired along with glycogenolysis in the liver in glycogen storage disease type I (Von Gierke disease). questions.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother 1 day after he had severe leg cramps while playing soccer. The mother says that he also has a 2-month history of fatigue and clumsiness, and that his face lacks expression. He tires easily with exercise. He has a 3-year history of migraine. He is at the 60th percentile for height and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows bilateral ptosis and limited vertical and horizontal gaze. His speech is slightly slurred. Examination of a muscle biopsy specimen shows ragged red fibers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Mitochondrial myopathies are a group of disorders characterized by neurologic and muscular symptoms, mitochondrial inheritance, and ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy. The disorders include chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO); Kearns-Sayre syndrome; mitochondrial myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS syndrome); and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF syndrome). The mitochondrial myopathies are caused by mutations in a variety of mitochondrial enzymes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, or in mitochondrial RNA, RNA translation, trafficking and incorporation of respiratory protein complexes, and maintenance of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Failure of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation results in reduced availability of ATP throughout the body, although muscle and nerve cells are particularly sensitive to a reduced supply of ATP. Patients typically present in childhood or adolescence with symptoms that are unique to each disorder, although findings generally include neurologic features such as cognitive impairment, epilepsy, stroke, ataxia, headache, hearing loss, and muscular findings such as ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, fatigue, muscle weakness, myoclonus, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Treatment of mitochondrial myopathies is primarily supportive. The prognosis varies widely across the group of disorders; some, such as MELAS syndrome, are typically fatal by adulthood, while others, such as CPEO, are associated with a normal life expectancy. Early diagnosis and appropriate supportive treatment are essential, as mortality caused by cardiac conduction defects can be prevented with implantation of a pacemaker.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Becker muscular dystrophy (Choice A) is a disorder of progressive muscle degeneration caused by X-linked recessive mutations in the DMD gene encoding dystrophin. It presents with progressive proximal muscular weakness, muscular atrophy, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower sign when standing, and respiratory distress. While closely related to Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Choice B), which is also caused by mutations in DMD and which presents with similar findings, Becker muscular dystrophy is characterized by a milder course, with most patients living to the fourth or fifth decade of life. In contrast, Duchenne muscular dystrophy is characterized by a progressive course with most patients dying of respiratory failure in the third decade of life.

Myotonic dystrophy (Choice D) is a genetic disorder caused by expansion of a trinucleotide repeat characterized by muscle weakness, myotonia, cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac arrhythmias, and hypogonadism. The most frequently affected muscles include the facial muscles, sternocleidomastoids, distal forearm muscles, intrinsic hand muscles, and ankle dorsiflexors.

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 1 (Choice E) is a particularly severe disease within the spectrum of SMA disorders, which are caused by mutations in the SMN1 gene. SMA is a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by motor neuron degeneration and resultant progressive hypotonia and areflexia. Patients with SMA exhibit difficulty with mobility and frequently experience respiratory distress and difficulty feeding. SMA type 1, also known as Werdnig-Hoffman SMA, is a severe, infantile-onset form of SMA that leads to hypotonia and respiratory failure within the first 6 months of life. Treatment is primarily supportive.

Educational Objective: Mitochondrial myopathies are a group of disorders characterized by neurologic and muscular symptoms, mitochondrial inheritance, and ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy. They are caused by mutations in mitochondrial enzymes involved in oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial function. Treatment is primarily supportive.

questions.stemHtml: During a study of exercise physiology, a healthy 30-year-old woman runs on a treadmill for 20 minutes at a rate of 7 miles per hour. At the end of the study, her cardiac output has increased from 5 L/min to 15 L/min; the cerebral perfusion pressure has remained relatively constant. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these findings?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Cardiac output (CO) influences mean arterial pressure (MAP) via the following relationship: MAP = CO × SVR, where SVR is systemic vascular resistance. In most organs, when CO increases, MAP can be kept relatively stable by decreasing SVR. This is accomplished by relaxation of the arteriolar wall smooth muscle, which leads to vasodilation. When CO decreases, arterioles constrict and increase SVR, maintaining MAP. Under physiologic conditions, this variation in pressure and blood flow is accommodated by end organs. However, the compliance of the intracranial compartment and its contents are limited by the fixed, rigid space of the skull. Strict autoregulation of pressures inside this space is critical for maintenance of appropriate perfusion pressure to the brain. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is one of the primary determining factors of cerebral blood flow. CPP is the difference between intracranial pressure (ICP) and MAP, expressed as: CPP = MAP–ICP. While mathematically, MAP can have a significant influence on CPP, cerebral autoregulation maintains CPP at a relatively stable level over a wide range of MAP (60 to 160 mm Hg in normotensive individuals). This is accomplished with vasoconstriction (myogenic arteriolar constriction) when MAP increases and vasodilation when MAP decreases.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Decreased intracranial pressure (Choice A) can be achieved by shifting cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into the spinal subarachnoid space or over a longer period of time, decreasing CSF production or increasing CSF reabsorption (Choice B). However, normal ICP ranges from 5 to 15 mm Hg. The influence it exerts on CPP is small relative to that of arteriolar pressure and is mitigated by autoregulation. Changes in CSF dynamics will therefore not have a large effect on CPP under physiologic conditions.

Increased venous drainage (Choice C) can enhance blood flow in other organs during exercise, but it is not a mechanism by which CPP is regulated. Venular tone has a lesser influence on MAP compared to arteriolar tone as there are minimal vascular smooth muscles in venules compared to arterioles.

Reflex bradycardia (Choice E) is a mechanism by which MAP can be maintained during a significant increase in SVR. CO is affected by heart rate (HR) via the following equation: CO = SV × HR, where SV is stroke volume. Just like MAP, HR has little effect on CPP provided that MAP remains within the autoregulatory range. Extreme bradycardia or tachycardia leading to severe hypotension could decrease CPP.

Educational Objective: Because of cerebral autoregulation, changes in cardiac output have minimal impact on cerebral blood flow. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is maintained at a nearly constant level over a wide range of mean arterial pressure. Only blood pressures below or above the autoregulatory range of 60 to 160 mm Hg will affect CPP.

questions.stemHtml: An 84-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after an episode of syncope. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 4-cm myxoma occupying the majority of the left atrium. The tumor will be excised using a robotically assisted operation via an oblique right atriotomy and transection of the interatrial septum. When making the incision into the left atrium to remove the myxoma, which of the following regions of the interatrial septum should be avoided in order to prevent injury to the cardiac conduction system?

options.label: C
options.html: C.  Posteroinferior region above the opening of the coronary sinus

options.label: D
options.html: D.  Superoanterior region above the limbus of the fossa ovalis

options.label: E
options.html: E.  Superoposterior region posterior to the fossa ovalis

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Normal cardiac conduction starts with an electrical impulse in the sinoatrial (SA) node located in the right atrium, which is depicted on a rhythm strip as the “P wave.” The electrical impulse is conducted throughout the atria, causing coordinated contraction of the right and left atria, with consequent active filling of the right and left ventricles. The electrical impulse also reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node located in the interatrial septum. Conduction is temporarily halted in the AV node to allow for complete active and passive filling of the ventricles, followed by conduction of the electrical impulse down the His-Purkinje system in the interventricular septum, then to the right and left bundle, and finally to the myocardial cells of the ventricles. This results in contraction of the right and left ventricles (QRS complex) with expulsion of blood into the pulmonary and systemic circulations, respectively. The ventricles subsequently repolarize (T wave) and relax to allow filling for the next cardiac cycle. The AV node is located in the posteroinferior region of the interatrial septum, more specifically, within Koch’s triangle, which is formed by the opening of the coronary sinus, septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve, and membranous portion of the interatrial septum. Injury to the AV node may result in AV block, a conduction abnormality that that ranges in severity from benign prolongation of the PR interval (first-degree AV block) to dissociation between atrial and ventricular impulses (third-degree AV block), a life-threatening condition requiring prompt intervention with a pacemaker.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

The crista terminalis (Choice A) is a curved ridge in the posterolateral wall of the right atrium, not in the interatrial septum, that courses between the superior and inferior vena caval orifices. It corresponds with a groove in the external aspect of the right atrial wall known as the terminal sulcus. The SA node is located in the right atrial wall between these two structures.

The fossa ovalis region (Choice B) is a remnant of the foramen ovale, an opening in the interatrial septum that allows blood to shunt from the right to left atria in the fetal heart. After birth, fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum closes the foramen ovale and forms the fossa ovalis. Failure of closure results in a patent foramen ovale (PFO). The fossa ovalis (or a PFO, if present) can be transected to safely access the left atrium.

The superoanterior region above the limbus of the fossa ovalis (Choice D) contains the Bachmann bundle before it leaves the interatrial septum to course along the left atrial wall. It is one of several pathways that allow electrical impulses to spread from the right to left atrium.

The superoposterior region posterior to the fossa ovalis (Choice E) is the location of the beginning of the anterior internodal conduction pathway; transection of this region may result in damage to this pathway, but the majority of internodal conduction would likely still be intact via the middle and posterior internodal pathways.


Educational Objective: Electrical impulses originate from the sinoatrial node, located in the right atrium, and reach the atrioventricular (AV) node, located in the interatrial septum, before being carried to the ventricles via the His-Purkinje system. When transecting the interatrial septum for access to the left atrium, care must be taken to avoid injuring the cardiac conduction system, most importantly, the AV node, which is located in the posteroinferior region of the septum above the opening of the coronary sinus.

questions.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man who has had no medical care for more than 10 years comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of intermittent episodes of dizziness and feeling faint. He says the symptoms are worse when he rises after lying down. He is unable to be even moderately physically active because of the dizziness. He has had no chest pain or shortness of breath during this period. His pulse is 30/min, respirations are 15/min, and supine blood pressure is 100/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. An ECG is shown. This patient most likely has which of the following dysrhythmias?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

Third-degree atrioventricular (AV) block (complete heart block) occurs when no sinus impulses are transmitted through the AV conduction pathway resulting in complete dissociation between the atria and ventricles, marked by no relationship between P waves and the QRS complexes on ECG. ECG will show a constant, regular interval between P waves and a different constant, regular interval between QRS complexes, which will show no relationship to one another. Patients with a third-degree AV block may present with fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, lightheadedness, or syncope. Causes include ischemic or structural heart disease, electrolyte abnormalities, systemic diseases (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, connective tissue disorders, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis), Lyme carditis, and medication toxicity. Any symptomatic patient requires intervention with chronotropic agents (eg, atropine, dopamine, epinephrine) though such agents may not resolve the symptoms. If the patient’s bradycardia is refractory to medical management, or if the patient becomes or remains hemodynamically unstable, transcutaneous or transvenous pacing should be performed. Definitive management includes reversal of any secondary causes, and placement of a permanent pacemaker in cases where no reversible cause is present.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

Atrial fibrillation (Choice A) and atrial flutter (Choice B) are both tachyarrhythmias that often present with palpitations, fatigue, lightheadedness, and dyspnea when symptomatic. On electrocardiography, atrial fibrillation shows irregularly irregular RR intervals without discernible P waves. Atrial flutter appears as regular flutter waves with regular or irregular QRS complexes, depending on the AV conduction ratio.

Second-degree atrioventricular block (Choice C) has two presentations: type I and type II. Second degree AV block type I is identified by a prolonged PR interval that progressively increases followed by a non-conducted P wave (no QRS), with resumption of normal conduction. It is usually benign. Second degree AV block type II is identified by a prolonged PR interval that does not progressively increase with intermittent non-conducted P waves. Treatment for type II often involves placement of a pacemaker.

Sinus arrest (Choice D) occurs when there is an absence of SA nodal activity for 3 seconds or longer. ECG will show absence of electrical activity followed by one or more escape beats.

Sinus bradycardia (Choice E), when symptomatic, may have a similar clinical presentation to that of a third-degree AV block with fatigue, dyspnea, and lightheadedness. In sinus bradycardia, conduction occurs in the typical fashion from the SA node to the AV node. ECG shows regular QRS complexes that are each preceded by a P wave, with a pulse  less than 60/min.

Educational Objective: Third-degree atrioventricular (AV) block occurs when no sinus impulses are transmitted through the AV conduction pathway resulting in complete dissociation between the P waves and the QRS complexes. Definitive management is placement of a permanent pacemaker or treatment of the underlying cause. Any unstable patient may require temporary electrical pacing or pharmacologic chronotropic support regardless of etiology.

questions.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-month history of episodes of severe abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. Abdominal examination shows epigastric tenderness to palpation without rebound tenderness or guarding. Serum studies show a triglyceride concentration of 2000 mg/dL, amylase activity of 2000 U/L, and lipase activity of 1800 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography shows no evidence of biliary tract obstruction. A drug from which of the following classes is most appropriate to treat this patient's lipid abnormality?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

This patient presents with recurrent epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, in the setting of hypertriglyceridemia, a known risk factor for acute interstitial pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis typically presents with epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back, nausea, and emesis. The patient often has a history of gallstones, alcohol use disorder, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia. Less common clinical manifestations are bruising of the flanks (Turner sign) and bruising around the umbilicus (Cullen sign). Acute pancreatitis can be complicated by necrosis, hemorrhage, abscess, or the formation of pseudocysts. Laboratory studies often show increased amylase and lipase activity. Recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis may lead to chronic pancreatitis and insufficiency of both the exocrine and endocrine pancreas. Any modifiable inciting causes of pancreatitis (eg, gallstones, alcohol use disorder, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia) should be mitigated to delay disease progression and preserve remaining native pancreatic function. The first-line class of medications to target hypertriglyceridemia in the absence of concomitant hypercholesterolemia (eg, increased serum LDL cholesterol concentration) is fibric acid derivatives. For example, gemfibrozil is a fibrate-based lipid-lowering agent that activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPAR) and upregulates lipoprotein lipase, resulting in decreased serum LDL, increased HDL, and decreased triglyceride concentrations.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Bile acid sequestrant (Choice A) medications form a nonabsorbable complex with bile acids in the gastrointestinal tract and facilitate their excretion in the stool. They are a second-line class used in hyperlipidemia after initiation of a statin. They are not used primarily in the management of hypertriglyceridemia.

Cholesterol absorption inhibitor (Choice B) medications are used to prevent micellar uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol in the small intestine. By limiting the amount of cholesterol that returns to the liver in chylomicrons, the liver upregulates LDL receptors which results in increased serum clearance of cholesterol. Ezetimibe is an example and is used in conjunction with statin medications in the treatment of hyperlipidemia.

HMG-CoA inhibitor (Choice D) medications are those that make up the “statin” group. By limiting hepatic synthesis of cholesterol, hepatic uptake of cholesterols from the bloodstream is increased. Statins are the first-line medications used in the treatment of hypercholesterolemia, especially for patients with increased LDL and decreased HDL cholesterol. They lower triglyceride concentrations as well, though to a lesser extent than their LDL-lowering capability. As a result, they are a second-line treatment to fibric acid derivatives for hypertriglyceridemia.

Omega-3 fatty acids (Choice E) have been studied for several decades as a means of reducing cardiovascular risk, though as of 2022, several reviews and meta-analyses have been published that show limited efficacy in certain populations. There is consensus that they may act to lower blood pressure and serum triglyceride concentrations without significantly changing serum LDL and HDL concentrations; however according to the consensus statement from the American Heart Association, their use is more appropriate at mild-to-moderate hypertriglyceridemia (triglyceride concentration in the 100-499 mg/dL range). Triglyceride levels above 500 mg/dL are best treated with fibric acid derivatives as a first-line agent.

Educational Objective: Acute pancreatitis typically presents with epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back, along with nausea and emesis, and often in a patient with a history of gallstones, alcoholism, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia. Risk factors should be addressed and treated to prevent recurrence of symptoms and limit the likelihood of progression to chronic pancreatitis. Hypertriglyceridemia is best treated with fibric acid derivatives as first-line agents.

questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive loss of peripheral vision. Ophthalmologic examination shows bitemporal hemianopia with normal fundi and visual acuity. A sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the brain with contrast is shown; the arrow indicates an abnormality. To surgically access and resect the mass via a nasal approach, which of the following sinuses must be traversed?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

This patient’s finding of progressive bitemporal hemianopia is consistent with a diagnosis of a pituitary mass lesion. Benign adenomas are the most common neoplasms identified in the pituitary gland, and may secrete hormones, such as prolactin or growth hormone, causing symptoms of hyperpituitarism. More commonly, pituitary mass lesions do not cause hyperpituitarism but instead cause compression of normal pituitary neurons, leading to hypopituitarism and dysfunction of multiple endocrine axes. The pituitary gland rests in the bony sella turcica, just inferior to the optic chiasm. Retinal ganglion cell fibers from the nasal retina, which supply the temporal visual fields, decussate at the chiasm, and are vulnerable to compression by pituitary mass lesions. Since the decussating nasal retinal fibers carry information from the temporal visual fields, the resultant visual field deficit is commonly a bitemporal hemianopia, a finding suggestive of a pituitary mass. Symptomatic pituitary mass lesions that require resection can be surgically approached via the sphenoid sinuses. The sphenoid sinuses are the most posterior of the paranasal sinuses, bordered anteriorly by the nasal cavity, superiorly by the hypophyseal fossa, and inferiorly by the pterygoid canal and nasopharynx. The sinus is accessed via the nose with osteotomy of the anteroinferior aspect of the sphenoid bone; the thin bone of the superior aspect of the sphenoid sinus is then pierced to enter the hypophyseal fossa.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, and C.

The ethmoid (Choice A) sinus is a complex structure of air cells, located inferior to the frontal bone and anterior cranial fossa, and medial to the orbit. It does not provide a straightforward access route to the pituitary fossa.

The frontal (Choice B) sinus is bordered by the anterior cranial fossa superiorly and posteriorly; orbit, ethmoid air cells, and nasal cavity inferiorly; and the contralateral frontal sinus medially. It does not provide a straightforward access route to the pituitary fossa.

The maxillary (Choice C) sinus is bordered by the orbit superiorly, maxillary alveolar bone inferiorly, nasal cavity medially, zygomas laterally and anteriorly, and pterygopalatine fossa and infratemporal fossa posteriorly. It does not provide a straightforward access route to the pituitary fossa.

Educational Objective: Pituitary mass lesions can compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia. Surgical resection of pituitary mass lesions can be accomplished via a transsphenoidal approach. The sinus is accessed via the nose with osteotomy of the anteroinferior aspect of the sphenoid bone; the thin bone of the superior aspect of the sphenoid sinus is then pierced to enter the hypophyseal fossa.

questions.stemHtml: An investigator studying bronchial circulation interrupts this circulation in experimental animals. As a result, which of the following processes is most likely to be affected?

options.label: C
options.html: C.  Delivery of nutrients to the tracheal wall

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Blood flow to the lungs is accomplished via two systems: the bronchial and the pulmonary circulations. The bronchial circulation is a branch of the high-pressure systemic circulation. It delivers oxygenated blood and nutrients to tracheobronchial structures of the conducting zone (eg, the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles), visceral pleura, and hilar lymph nodes. Respiratory tree structures in the respiratory zone (eg, the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar sacs) derive nutrients from mixed venous blood of the pulmonary circulation and are oxygenated by direct diffusion from air. As with any other branch of the systemic circulation, low Po2 causes hypoxic vasodilation to help meet the demand of the target tissue. There are usually two left bronchial arteries, which arise from the thoracic aorta, and one right bronchial artery, which usually arises from an intercostal artery. While some venous drainage is carried by bronchial veins, most of it is carried out of the lungs by pulmonary veins, creating a physiologic right-to-left shunt. Occlusion of the bronchial circulation will therefore disrupt oxygen and nutrient delivery to tracheal parenchyma but will not disrupt the special functions carried out by the pulmonary circulation.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system originating from the pulmonary trunk. It delivers deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary capillary bed interacts with the alveoli for gas exchange and the venous network returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Additionally, the pulmonary circulation provides nutrients for lung parenchymal cells in the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar sacs. Thus, disruption of the pulmonary, not bronchial circulation could disrupt alveolar macrophage production (Choice A), as well as surfactant production (Choice E), which is carried out by type II pneumocytes in the alveoli. The high elasticity and permeability of these vessels can predispose them to extravasation of fluid into the interstitial space and alveoli when this low-pressure system cannot overcome the higher pressure of the left atrium downstream. Clearance of pulmonary edema (Choice B) is performed by absorption of this fluid back into this circulatory bed. A unique feature of the pulmonary circulation is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (Choice D). In contrast to systemic bronchial circulation, pulmonary vessels constrict in response to low Po2, shunting deoxygenated blood away from poorly ventilated portions of the lung and toward well-ventilated portions of the lung to maximize gas exchange into the circulation.

Educational Objective: The lungs contain a dual circulatory supply via the bronchial and pulmonary systems. The bronchial system is a branch of the high-pressure systemic circulation that delivers oxygen and nutrients to the tracheobronchial tree to the level of the terminal bronchioles, visceral pleura, and hilar lymph nodes. The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system involved in gas exchange with the alveoli, oxygenation of blood, supply of nutrients to specialized alveolar cells, and clearance of pulmonary edema.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the office because of a 2-week history of progressive shortness of breath. He had smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years before quitting 1 year ago. Current medications include albuterol as needed. His respirations are 18/min. Physical examination shows wheezing. Pulmonary function testing shows an FEV1 that is 55% of predicted value compared with 65% 1 year ago. It is most appropriate to add a drug to this patient's medication regimen that binds to or interferes with which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is an obstructive lung disease characterized by decreased lung function from a combination of features of chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema. This results in airflow obstruction on expiration, especially in a patient with history of tobacco use. In general, the goals of therapy are to reduce symptom severity, improve quality of life, and prevent exacerbations and hospitalizations. This is achieved with pharmacologic agents that modulate airway tone and inflammatory response, primarily muscarinic antagonists, β-adrenergic agonists, and glucocorticoids. Albuterol is a short-acting β-adrenergic agonist typically employed as a first-line agent for symptom management. If symptoms persist, as for this patient, addition of a short-acting muscarinic antagonist is the next recommended step. Airway smooth muscle tone is increased by cholinergic signaling. Inhibition of muscarinic receptors in the lungs results in smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F.

β-Adrenoreceptors (Choice A) are stimulated by β-adrenergic agonists, which are effective in treating symptoms of asthma and COPD as they cause airway smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation. This patient is already prescribed a β-adrenergic agonist, and medication targeting muscarinic receptors should be the next step.

Interleukin-1 (IL-1) synthesis (Choice B) is implicated in the pathogenesis of asthma and COPD as a primary inflammatory mediator that results in airway narrowing over time.

Medications that inhibit leukotriene receptors (Choice C), such as montelukast, are used in the treatment of asthma and allergic rhinitis, but do not have strong evidence yet for improvement in COPD outcomes.

Mast cell degranulation (Choice D) is inhibited by antihistamines, commonly used in treatment of allergies and anaphylaxis. They are not typically used for management of asthma or COPD.

Phosphodiesterase (Choice F) inhibitors, particularly phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4), are used in severe, refractory COPD as they decrease airway inflammation and promote smooth muscle relaxation. Roflumilast is an example. These medications are typically reserved for patients who have failed regimens that include short- and long-acting β-adrenergic agonists, muscarinic antagonists, and glucocorticoids.

Educational Objective: Long- and short-acting muscarinic antagonists, β-adrenergic agonists, and glucocorticoids are the mainstays of treatment for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Muscarinic antagonists and β-adrenergic agonists promote airway smooth muscle relaxation causing bronchodilation and less resistance to air flow.

questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man who is a retired coal miner comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath. He also has had a 23-kg (50-lb) weight loss during this period. He appears cachectic. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and now weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 137/83 mm Hg. Physical examination shows symmetric air entry with no crackles or wheezes. A chest x-ray and photomicrograph of lung tissue obtained on biopsy are shown. The structure indicated by the arrow in the photomicrograph most likely represents which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

The patient’s presentation and diagnostic studies are consistent with a diagnosis of interstitial lung disease (ILD). ILD encompasses a heterogeneous group of disorders that result in pulmonary fibrosis and progressively impaired lung function. Patients classically present with progressive dyspnea and chronic non-productive cough. The underlying cause is often determined clinically from the patient’s presentation, imaging patterns, and exposure history; however, lung biopsy can provide a definitive diagnosis. The photomicrograph shows a silicotic nodule, with the characteristic central spiral appearance from layered, concentric collagen fiber deposition. Surrounding this central region is a less organized, whorled zone containing macrophages, lymphocytes, and loosely formed collagen. These lesions are pathognomonic for silicosis, which commonly affects workers in the mining, sandblasting, glass manufacturing, and foundry industries. Inhaled crystalline silica dust particles are deposited in the terminal bronchioles and alveoli, resulting in macrophage activation and inflammatory changes. Patients are at increased risk for developing pulmonary tuberculosis and primary lung cancer.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Aspergillus species hyphae (Choice A) may be seen in invasive aspergillosis, aspergilloma, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. These syndromes tend to present with hemoptysis, wheezing, fever, and cough.

Fibrinogen (Choice C) is the precursor for fibrin, the primary structural component that makes up clot in coagulation and hemostasis. The photomicrograph shows a rounded lesion of dense, layered collagen fibers, consistent with silicosis.

Hyaline membranes (Choice D) are observed in the setting of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which is characterized by the rapid onset of diffuse inflammatory lung injury. Histologic examination shows diffuse alveolar damage with leakage of protein-rich material into the alveolar space, lining it with a hyaline membrane. The disease may progress to diffuse interstitial fibrosis.

Microabscess (Choice E) on histologic examination appears as fibrosis surrounding pus composed of necrotic tissue debris and microorganisms, typically with a thickened fibrinous outer wall.
Educational Objective: Silicosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust particles, which are deposited in the terminal bronchioles and alveoli. Silicotic nodules are characterized by a central hyaline core made of concentrically layered collagen fibers, surrounded by a less organized zone of inflammatory cells and loose collagen.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman with primary pulmonary hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Her blood pressure is 190/100 mm Hg. Echocardiography shows a peak pulmonary systolic pressure of 65 mm Hg. Treatment with bosentan is started. This therapy is most likely to result in blockade of the action of which of the following peptides in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Bosentan is a competitive endothelin-1 antagonist that is used for the treatment of primary pulmonary arterial hypertension. Two clinically relevant subtypes of endothelin receptors are the endothelin A (ETA) and the endothelin B (ETB) receptors. Binding of endothelin-1 to ETA results in vasoconstriction, whereas binding of endothelin-1 to ETB results in production of nitric oxide and vasodilation. In the context of pulmonary arterial hypertension, the aggregate effect of endothelin-1 results in vasoconstriction and an increase in pulmonary vascular resistance. Bosentan competitively antagonizes the binding of endothelin-1 to both ETA and ETB receptors. However, its greater affinity for ETA results in a vasodilatory effect and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance, limiting pulmonary hypertension, and relieving strain on the right side of the heart. Bosentan is hepatotoxic; patients treated with bosentan should be monitored for increases of serum transaminases.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Calcitonin gene−related peptide (Choice A) is a ubiquitous neuropeptide involved in neuroendocrine signaling. It is involved in modulation of pancreatic hormone secretion and glucose regulation.

Neuropeptide Y (Choice C) is an orexigenic peptide neurotransmitter that is active in many parts of the central nervous system, especially neurons of the sympathetic nervous system and the hypothalamus. Neuropeptide Y signaling is associated with vasoconstriction, modulation of appetite and metabolism, and regulation of circadian rhythms. It is not associated with pulmonary hypertension.

Substance P (Choice D) is a peptide neurotransmitter that is involved in nociception in the peripheral nervous system. Though it is observed to have a potent vasodilatory effect when exposed to vascular tissue, it is not used in the treatment of pulmonary hypertension.

Urotensin II (Choice E) is a cyclic peptide and potent vasoconstrictor that is typically associated with cardiovascular and endocrine disease. It is implicated in the pathophysiology of metabolic syndrome, as well as cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity.

questions.stemHtml: A previously healthy 59-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever, shortness of breath, and productive cough. He appears to be in moderate distress. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and respirations are 26/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Bronchial breath sounds are heard over the right lung base posteriorly with egophony and increased tactile fremitus. A chest x-ray shows right lower lobe pneumonia. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of the hypoxia in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

The cause of hypoxemia can be divided into five categories: hypoventilation, low inspired partial pressure of oxygen, right-to-left shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and diffusion impairment across the alveolar-capillary interface. Identifying the category can help in narrowing the differential diagnosis for the underlying disease state. Clinical history and measurement of the alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient on arterial blood gas analysis can direct the clinician to the correct category. In this case, the presence of fever, shortness of breath, productive cough, and infiltrate on chest x-ray are sufficient for a diagnosis of pneumonia. In pneumonia, the alveolar space and bronchioles become filled with fluid and/or pus. These regions do not participate in gas exchange as they cannot be ventilated. The pulmonary vasculature responds with hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which restricts blood flow from the hypoxic regions of lung to match areas of sufficient perfusion with areas of sufficient ventilation. In pneumonia and other disease states, this mechanism can be overwhelmed leading to ventilation-perfusion mismatch and subsequent hypoxemia.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Alveolar fibrosis (Choice A) can be caused by many diseases due to recurrent inflammatory injury. Fibrosis reduces the total surface area of the alveolar-capillary interface that participates in gas exchange, eventually leading to hypoxemia. This falls into the diffusion impairment category of hypoxemia causes.

Hypoventilation (Choice B) results when a patient has an inadequate minute volume to clear carbon dioxide. The increased partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the alveoli decreases the amount of oxygen available for diffusion, resulting in hypoxemia. Diffusion and perfusion are not directly affected. Hypoventilation occurs in patients with central nervous system depression and neuromuscular disease, in which the body’s ability to move air in and out of the lungs is impaired.

Right-to-left cardiac shunt (Choice C) occurs when deoxygenated venous blood mixes with the systemic circulation without passing through the pulmonary vasculature, resulting in hypoxemia. In pneumonia, perfusion through the lungs is normal, while ventilation is impaired due to airway and alveolar obstruction.

Right ventricular failure (Choice D) results in hypoxemia because of reduced cardiac output through the pulmonary vasculature. Hypoxemia results from ventilation-perfusion mismatch. This patient’s clinical presentation is more consistent with pneumonia.

Educational Objective: The cause of hypoxemia can be divided into five categories: hypoventilation, low inspired partial pressure of oxygen, right-to-left shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and diffusion impairment across the alveolar-capillary interface. The alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient on arterial blood gas analysis is normal in hypoventilation and low inspired oxygen content, and increases in the setting of a shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and diffusion impairment.

questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of increasingly severe left-sided chest pain during the past 12 hours. The pain worsens on deep inspiration. He was moving furniture when the pain began. His father died of a myocardial infarction at the age of 58 years. His respirations are 18/min. Palpation over the costochondral junction to the left of the sternum reproduces the pain. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

This patient’s acute, well-localized chest wall pain with accompanying tenderness to palpation of the affected area is consistent with costochondritis. Costochondritis is a common cause of chest wall pain and involves inflammation of the costochondral or chondrosternal joints of the thoracic rib cage. Costochondritis is a self-limited condition and is usually idiopathic. While patients may present with symptoms that worsen during deep inspiration (due to chest wall expansion during inspiration), localized tenderness to palpation helps to differentiate costochondritis from other causes of pleuritic chest pain. Laboratory studies, x-rays, and ECGs are normal in costochondritis and generally only aid the diagnosis by excluding other potential diagnoses (eg, pneumonia, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism). Treatment for costochondritis involves non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications and physical therapy.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F.

Coronary artery disease (Choice A) resulting in a myocardial infarction classically presents with left-sided chest pain but would be abnormal in a young patient without predisposing factors. Generally, myocardial infarction does not cause tenderness upon palpation of the chest wall.

Pericarditis (Choice C) classically presents with substernal chest pain, which is often pleuritic, worse when lying down, and improves with leaning forward. It can occur secondary to inflammatory, infectious, or malignant conditions. The ribs are not usually tender to palpation.

Pleurisy (Choice D), or inflammation of the pleura, can cause chest pain. It can be caused by pneumonia, which presents with signs and symptoms including fever, chills, shortness of breath, productive cough, and tachypnea, all of which are absent in this patient.

Pulmonary embolism (Choice E) is characteristically associated with long periods of immobilization such as orthopedic surgery, intensive care unit stay, long drives, and long plane flights, due to the association with deep venous thrombosis formation from venous stasis. Classic symptoms include chest pain and dyspnea; if an infarction has occurred, pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis may be present. Vital signs are often notable for tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Hypotension can be present if the embolus is large enough to obstruct blood flow from the right ventricle.

Rib fracture (Choice F) is a common cause of acute chest pain in younger patients, who are more likely to sustain injuries from trauma (eg, car accident, sports). The injured area is tender to external palpation. Rib fractures are rarely spontaneous and are unlikely in a patient who lacks a history of trauma.

Educational Objective: Costochondritis, inflammation of the costochondral or chondrosternal junctions, presents with respirophasic chest pain and focal tenderness to palpation, often in a younger person without risk factors for cardiac, pulmonary, or vascular causes of pain.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of fatigue. Six months ago, she visited family in Brazil, where she was exposed to domestic and farm animals. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for pallor. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 7.2 g/dL and a hematocrit of 23%. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Hookworm infection is widespread in the developing world and is a common cause of anemia. Infection is typically caused by the parasitic roundworms Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. Juvenile hookworms hatch from eggs in soil and are capable of penetrating intact human skin. Exposure typically occurs while walking barefoot on contaminated soil. Once the hookworm has entered the host, it travels through the bloodstream to the lungs, enters the alveoli, and migrates to the trachea and oropharynx, from where it is swallowed. The worm then enters the gastrointestinal tract, where it matures and lays eggs that are fecally excreted. Patients may be asymptomatic, but signs and symptoms may include fatigue, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and anemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by identification of eggs or adult worms on stool microscopy. Treatment is with oral albendazole. Albendazole binds to beta-tubulin and inhibits microtubule polymerization. This has a variety of vermicidal effects, including prevention of glucose utilization, glycogen depletion, and inhibition of cellular motility and cellular division. Patients with anemia may benefit from oral iron supplementation while the disease process resolves.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Enterobius vermicularis (Choice A) is a parasitic helminth that causes pinworm infection. Pinworm infection is spread by fecal-oral transmission and can cause intense, typically nocturnal, anal and peri-anal pruritus. Treatment is with albendazole.

Schistosoma mansoni (Choice C) is a parasitic flatworm that is responsible for intestinal schistosomiasis. It is transmitted by contact with fresh water contaminated by infected snails. Symptoms may be mild or severe and include abdominal pain, diarrhea, hematochezia, abdominal distension, and bowel obstruction. Treatment is with oral praziquantel.

Taenia solium (Choice D) is a parasitic tapeworm that causes cysticercosis. Cysticercosis can affect nearly every organ system through larval invasion of tissues. Frequent manifestations include subcutaneous nodules, muscle pain, vision loss, and central nervous system (CNS) symptoms. Involvement of the CNS is known as neurocysticercosis and may present with seizures, headache, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. Treatment is with oral praziquantel or albendazole.

Trichuris trichiura (Choice E) is parasitic roundworm that causes trichuriasis, also known as whipworm infection. The organism is endemic to tropical regions throughout the world. Symptoms may include abdominal pain and distension, diarrhea, hematochezia, and iron deficiency anemia. Treatment is with oral ivermectin plus a benzimidazole, such as albendazole or mebendazole.

Educational Objective: Hookworm infection, usually caused by Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus, is widespread in the developing world and is a common cause of anemia. Exposure typically occurs while walking barefoot on contaminated soil. Patients may be asymptomatic, but signs and symptoms may include fatigue, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and anemia. Treatment is with oral albendazole and iron supplementation.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressive loss of appetite and difficulty swallowing. His last medical examination was 10 years ago. He has taken calcium carbonate for chronic heartburn and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for joint aches for the past 10 years. He drinks approximately four to five 12-ounce beers daily. His diet consists primarily of meat and simple carbohydrates. He appears cachectic. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows a stricture at the esophagogastric junction. Examination of a biopsy specimen of the esophagus shows adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing risk factor for this patient's condition?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Chronic heartburn, or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), commonly occurs because of increased intra-abdominal pressure related to obesity or diminished closing pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter, permitting acidic contents of the stomach to reflux into the esophagus. Chronic GERD may cause intestinal metaplasia of the lower esophagus, which predisposes patients to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Esophageal adenocarcinoma typically presents with progressive dysphagia because of the mass effect of the tumor. Initially, the mass is small enough to only obstruct the passage of large, solid foods. As the mass enlarges, passage of all solids becomes affected, along with some or all liquids. Nonspecific signs of malignancy, such as weight loss, are also seen. Diagnosis can be made with upper endoscopy and biopsy. Direct extension of the malignancy or lymphadenopathy surrounding the neighboring structures may also cause symptoms. Esophageal adenocarcinoma may be treated with a combination of chemotherapy, radiation, and surgical resection.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Alcohol use (Choice A) is associated with squamous metaplasia of the cells lining the upper esophagus. Over time, squamous metaplasia may worsen and lead to the development of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus most commonly involves the upper two-thirds of the esophagus.

Gender (Choice C) and a low-fiber diet (Choice D) have not been linked to the development of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

NSAID use (Choice E) may cause gastritis but is not recognized as a direct proximate contributor to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Educational Objective: Chronic heartburn, or gastroesophageal reflux disease, may result in intestinal metaplasia of the lower esophagus and over time may predispose patients to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Patients with esophageal adenocarcinoma present with symptoms of weight loss and progressive dysphagia, and diagnosis is made with upper endoscopy and biopsy.

questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease undergoes upper endoscopy. Results show a 4-cm, bulging nodule in the stomach covered with an intact mucosal surface. The mass is subsequently resected, and examination shows that it is contained within the submucosa; it is fleshy and well circumscribed with minimal mucosal alterations. A diagnosis of gastrointestinal stromal tumor is made. Further examination of this tumor is most likely to show which of the following molecular alterations?

options.label: A
options.html: A.  Activation of the APC/β-catenin pathway

options.label: B
options.html: B.  Activation of KIT receptor tyrosine kinase

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are uncommon sarcomatous neoplasms, generally of the stomach and small intestine, that have malignant potential. They arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, part of the enteric nervous system. questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old man with a history of duodenal peptic ulcer disease has the sudden onset of severe epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. The abdomen is rigid, tightly distended, and hyperresonant. An x-ray of the abdomen shows air under both sides of the diaphragm. Which of the following structures is most likely involved with the patient's ulcer?

options.label: E
options.html: E.  Retroperitoneal portion of the duodenum

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Peptic ulcer disease describes the presence of ulcers in the stomach or duodenum, which classically present with worsening abdominal pain related to consumption (gastric) or lack of consumption (duodenal) of food. Persistent inflammation related to a peptic ulcer can result in complications including fibrosis, stricture, hemorrhage, and perforation. Anterior wall ulcers are associated with a higher risk for perforation, while posterior wall ulcers have an increased risk for hemorrhage given their position near the traversing gastroduodenal artery. Perforation commonly presents with acute abdominal pain, peritonitis, fever, and free air on x-ray and CT scan. This patient’s examination with hyperresonance and abdominal distension is suggestive of pneumoperitoneum, or air within the peritoneal cavity, which indicates the perforation likely occurred along the anterior duodenal wall.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

The ampulla of Vater (Choice A) is where the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct meet to drain into the duodenum. In pathology, obstruction at the ampulla from gallstone, stricture, or tumor blocks both the common bile duct, predisposing to ascending cholangitis, and the main pancreatic duct, predisposing to acute pancreatitis.

The celiac plexus (Choice C) is a network of nerves in the abdomen. It is typically located posterior to the stomach and would not likely be affected by a perforated duodenal ulcer.

The head of the pancreas (Choice D) is a potential site of pancreatic cancer. When there is a cancerous mass within the head of the pancreas, it commonly imposes mass effect upon the main pancreatic duct and common bile duct, leading to painless jaundice.

The duodenum’s first segment is intraperitoneal, but the second through fourth segments are retroperitoneal. A perforated ulcer in the retroperitoneal portion of the duodenum (Choice E) would be unlikely to result in pneumoperitoneum.

Educational Objective: Perforation of a duodenal ulcer is an emergent condition often presenting with acute abdominal pain, peritonitis, fever, and free air on x-ray and CT scan. Given the location of the duodenum at its different segments, perforation of the anterior duodenal wall can result in pneumoperitoneum, while posterior wall ulcers are more commonly associated with hemorrhage from the gastroduodenal artery.

questions.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of vomiting for 24 hours. He has a 1-week history of chronic constipation with bloating and abdominal pain. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 111 kg (245 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Abdominal examination of the left lower quadrant shows muscle guarding; palpation of this area produces pain. A CT scan of the abdomen shows diverticula. The diverticula are most likely present in which of the following regions of the gastrointestinal system in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

The sigmoid colon is the most common location for diverticula to form. Diverticula are outpouchings of the mucosal and submucosal layers into the muscular layer that occur at weak points in the gut wall where the small arterioles of the vasa recta penetrate. It is hypothesized that abnormal motility in the colon causes increased intraluminal pressure with subsequent herniation of the mucosa through weak points in the colonic wall. This may happen in the sigmoid colon because the diameter of the sigmoid is smaller than other parts of the colon, so abnormal peristalsis in this area causes higher intraluminal pressure compared to other segments. Risk factors for development of diverticula include obesity and a diet high in red meat and low in fiber. Diverticulosis predisposes to lower gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. It also predisposes to diverticulitis, a bacterial infection of a diverticulum that leads to a local inflammatory response. Diverticulitis presents classically with fever, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and occasionally with bloody diarrhea. Treatment includes bowel rest, symptomatic control, and antibiotics covering enteric flora.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Cecum (Choice A) is the most proximal portion of large bowel, a pouch near the ileum and the ascending colon. It is a less common a site of diverticulosis than the sigmoid. The appendix connects with it; as a result, the cecum can become inflamed in severe, acute appendicitis. Cecal diverticulitis would present with right-sided, not left-sided, abdominal pain and tenderness.

The descending colon (Choice B) and the rectum (Choice D) may develop diverticula, but these sites are less common than the sigmoid colon.

A Meckel diverticulum is commonly located in the ileum (Choice C), 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve. The diverticulum is approximately 2 inches in length. In children, it may serve as a potential lead-point for intussusception or as a site of GI bleeding. Discovery of it in adulthood without preceding pathology would be uncommon.

Educational Objective: Acute diverticulitis is infection and/or inflammation of existing colonic diverticula, which are small outpouchings of the bowel wall, commonly located in the sigmoid colon.

questions.stemHtml: A previously healthy 48-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of constant abdominal pain and fever. The pain radiates to the right shoulder and is accompanied by nausea and vomiting with no blood. She takes no medications. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She is in acute distress. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows marked tenderness of the right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding. Bowel sounds are decreased. Which of the following responses is expected in this patient on palpation of the right upper quadrant of the abdomen during the respiratory cycle?

options.label: A
options.html: A.  Decreased pain and expiratory arrest

options.label: B
options.html: B.  Decreased pain and inspiratory arrest

options.label: C
options.html: C.  Increased pain and expiratory arrest

options.label: D
options.html: D.  Increased pain and inspiratory arrest

options.label: E
options.html: E. No change in pain or respirations

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

This patient with right upper quadrant pain, vomiting, and fever has a presentation consistent with acute cholecystitis. Acute cholecystitis occurs secondary to obstruction of the cystic duct from a gallstone, which results in subsequent inflammation of the gallbladder wall. It typically presents with fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant. Increased pain and inspiratory arrest with palpation of the right subcostal area, known as Murphy sign, is present in acute cholecystitis. During inspiration, the abdominal organs are pushed downward, causing the gallbladder to come into contact with the examiner’s hand, leading to increased pain, which explains this finding. If gallstones migrate into the common bile duct, obstruction can lead to increased transaminase levels and a cholestatic pattern of liver injury with increased alkaline phosphatase. Right upper quadrant ultrasonography is the first-line diagnostic examination, and shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall, and pericholecystic fluid. A sonographic Murphy sign may be obtained, which is characterized by pain and tenderness elicited when the gallbladder is compressed by the ultrasound probe, while being visualized on the monitor. Treatment includes intravenous fluids, intravenous antibiotics, and cholecystectomy, in addition to appropriate supportive care with analgesics and antiemetics.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Decreased pain and expiratory arrest (Choice A) and increased pain and expiratory arrest (Choice C) would not be expected in a patient with cholecystitis. Inspiration, not expiration, is what causes the gallbladder to come into contact with the examiner’s hand, and this leads to the increase in pain.

Decreased pain and inspiratory arrest (Choice B) would not be expected in a patient with cholecystitis. Although inspiratory arrest is seen, it occurs because of the increase in pain that is occurring.

No change in pain or respirations (Choice E) would not be expected in a patient with cholecystitis.

Educational Objective: Acute cholecystitis is caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone, leading to inflammation and subsequent infection of the gallbladder. Presentation typically includes right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Increased pain and inspiratory arrest with palpation of the right subcostal area, known as Murphy Sign, is present in acute cholecystitis.
