questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 2 hours after the sudden onset of severe midepigastric abdominal pain. He vomited a small amount of bloody fluid shortly after the pain began. En route, his pulse is 150/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. Perforation of the duodenum is suspected. Which of the following sets of abdominal physical findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: A.  Absent bowel sounds, rigid abdominal wall, tenderness and guarding throughout

options.label: B
options.html: B. Active bowel sounds, distention, right lower quadrant tenderness and rebound

options.label: C
options.html: C.  Hyperactive bowel sounds, soft abdomen, no tenderness

options.label: D
options.html: D.  Hypoactive bowel sounds, distention, tenderness and guarding in the left lower quadrant

options.label: E
options.html: E.  Normal bowel sounds, enlarged tender liver, positive fluid wave

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

This patient with an acute onset of severe abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, and hypotension has a presentation consistent with a perforated abdominal viscus. When perforation occurs, bowel contents leak into the peritoneal cavity leading to widespread inflammation and translocation of bacteria into an otherwise sterile space. Patients with peritonitis often display characteristic examination findings of rebound tenderness, guarding, and abdominal wall rigidity. As inflammation progresses, a secondary ileus can occur, leading to hypoactive or absent bowel sounds. Upright chest and abdominal x-ray classically demonstrate free air under the diaphragm. If the patient is stable and diagnosis is uncertain, an abdominal CT scan can be obtained. Management in the emergency department includes resuscitation with crystalloid and early administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Perforated viscus with resultant peritonitis is a surgical emergency requiring exploratory laparotomy; surgical consultation should be obtained at the time a diagnosis of peritonitis is suspected.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Active bowel sounds, distention, right lower quadrant tenderness and rebound (Choice B) describe findings that may be seen in a patient with unruptured, acute appendicitis. Appendicitis also merits early surgical consultation and antibiotics, as appendectomy is curative if inflammation and infection remain contained within the appendix.

Hyperactive bowel sounds, soft abdomen, no tenderness (Choice C) describe findings that may be seen in a patient with gastroenteritis. Gastroenteritis generally arises from viral or bacterial infection and is often self-limited. Protracted cases, or those arising from invasive or inflammatory pathogens (eg, S. typhi) may require treatment with antibiotics. Supportive care is often all that is required in mild, viral cases.

Hypoactive bowel sounds, distention, tenderness and guarding in the left lower quadrant (Choice D) describe findings that may be seen in a patient with diverticulitis. Diverticulitis is inflammation or infection of colonic diverticula and is generally treated with oral antibiotics and symptom control in uncomplicated cases.

Normal bowel sounds, enlarged tender liver, positive fluid wave (Choice E) describe findings that may be seen in a patient with acute hepatitis. A positive fluid wave is seen in patients with ascites which occurs secondary to portal hypertension.

Educational Objective: Perforated abdominal viscus is a surgical emergency. Presentation includes severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and potential hemodynamic instability. Physical examination may disclose peritoneal signs such as rebound tenderness, guarding, and abdominal wall rigidity. Early surgical consultation is imperative for definitive management.

questions.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of flank and abdominal pain. A CT scan of the abdomen shows an aneurysm of the proximal portion of the superior mesenteric artery. This aneurysm is most likely to compress and impede venous blood flow from which of the following organs?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

The left renal vein courses just inferior to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) from the abdominal aorta before draining into the inferior vena cava (IVC). Compression of the left renal vein can occur when the angle between the SMA and aorta is abnormally small, or in the setting of a structural anomaly of the SMA such as aneurysm, as seen in this patient. Clinical manifestations include hematuria, flank pain, and orthostatic proteinuria. The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein distal to the point of compression. Thus, males can present with a left-sided varicocele or left testicular pain. Diagnosis can be confirmed with Doppler ultrasonography, CT angiography, or MR angiography. Children and adolescents can often be treated conservatively with observation, as the condition may resolve with further growth. ACE inhibitors can reduce orthostatic proteinuria. Adults and those with vascular anomalies may require surgical intervention to transpose or bypass the vein, or repair the anomaly, respectively. Compression of the renal vein by the SMA should not be confused with SMA syndrome, in which the duodenum is compressed between the SMA and aorta resulting in a proximal small bowel obstruction.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Liver (Choice B) is incorrect, as the hepatic veins emerge from the posterior surface of the liver and drain into the IVC. Local external compression of these vessels is not commonly seen because of their anatomic location and large caliber. Hepatic venous outflow obstruction can be caused by thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome) and presents with right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and increased serum liver enzymes.

Right kidney (Choice C) is incorrect, as the right renal vein drains directly into the IVC without passing near the SMA. questions.stemHtml: During an experiment, a drug that specifically dilates the efferent arterioles of the kidney is infused into an experimental animal. Which of the following sets of renal changes is most likely to occur in response to the drug?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: H.

Each nephron of the kidney contains a glomerulus, a network of capillaries where blood is filtered across capillary walls into the Bowman capsule; this filtrate subsequently proceeds into the renal tubules and eventually the collecting duct. Blood enters the glomerulus via an afferent arteriole, then exits via an efferent arteriole, which carries filtered blood away from the glomerulus. The efferent arteriole’s relative state of vasoconstriction or vasodilation affects the glomerular pressure and thus filtration within the glomerular capillaries. When the efferent arteriole constricts, blood flow is slowed, vascular resistance is increased, and the filtration fraction is increased. Increased filtration fraction in turn increases the amount of solute reaching the proximal tubule, which thus increases proximal tubule reabsorption. Dilation of the efferent arteriole has an opposite effect, resulting in a decreased filtration fraction and proximal tubule reabsorption secondary to decreased vascular resistance. Renal blood flow changes proportionate to the glomerular filtration rate and increases in renal blood flow result in an increase in renal O2 consumption. Dilation of the efferent arteriole decreases glomerular filtration rate, renal blood flow, and renal O2 consumption.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G.

Dilation of the efferent arterioles of the kidney causes decreased, not increased proximal tubule reabsorption (Choices A, B, and C), or unchanged proximal tubule reabsorption (Choices D and E). Renal O2 consumption and filtration fraction decreases, not increases, because of efferent arteriole dilation (Choice F).

Educational Objective: The efferent arteriole’s relative state of vasoconstriction or vasodilation affects the glomerular pressure and thus filtration within the glomerular capillaries. Efferent arteriole dilation results in decreased proximal tubule reabsorption, renal O2 consumption, and filtration fraction.

questions.stemHtml: An experimental animal receives a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. One hour later, which of the following sets of changes in plasma is most likely in this animal?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Carbonic anhydrase is an enzyme present in erythrocytes that catalyzes the conversion of carbon dioxide and water to bicarbonate (HCO3−) and hydrogen ions (H+). H+ binds to hemoglobin and modulates the unloading and loading of oxygen while HCO3− is exchanged out of the cell for chloride via a chloride/bicarbonate pump located on the cell surface. A deficiency in carbonic anhydrase activity leads to lower levels of intracellular bicarbonate, which would result in an influx of bicarbonate into the cell, resulting in decreased serum bicarbonate and a metabolic acidosis with a decreased pH. To counteract this, a respiratory alkalosis with resultant decreased Pco2 will result.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, F, G, and H.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibition will lead to a decrease, not an increase of serum bicarbonate levels (Choices A, B, C, and D). A decrease in serum bicarbonate levels leads to a metabolic acidosis, not metabolic alkalosis (Choices A, D, F, and H). A metabolic acidosis results in a compensatory respiratory alkalosis (partial pressure of carbon dioxide increases, not decreases, Choices A, B, G, and H).

Educational Objective: Carbonic anhydrase is an enzyme present in erythrocytes that catalyzes the conversion of carbon dioxide and water to bicarbonate (HCO3−) and hydrogen ions (H+). Carbonic anhydrase inhibition will lead to a metabolic acidosis and compensatory respiratory alkalosis.

questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit after having a myocardial infarction. During the next 36 hours, his serum creatinine concentration increases to 3.9 mg/dL and his urine output decreases. Three days later, he develops polyuria. At the time of discharge from the hospital, his serum creatinine concentration is 2.6 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's episode of acute kidney injury?

options.label: C
options.html: C.  Atheroembolic renal disease with acute renal infarction

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Decreased urinary output following a likely episode of hypotension in the setting of cardiac ischemia is consistent with a diagnosis of acute tubular necrosis (ATN). The cells of the proximal convoluted tubule, which are responsible for a large portion of ion resorption from the glomerular filtrate, are highly metabolically active and therefore are especially sensitive to ischemic injury. ATN progresses through an initial oliguric phase, which may last for several weeks before recovery, and is followed by a subsequent polyuric phase. Ischemic ATN may occur secondary to any type of shock state. In this patient, a myocardial infarction likely led to cardiogenic shock and hypotension, impairing renal perfusion. Cardiogenic, obstructive, hypovolemic, and distributive shock etiologies can all result in renal hypoperfusion. ATN may also occur secondary to nephrotoxic exposures such as heavy metals, antibiotics, and toxic alcohols. Urinalysis typically discloses muddy brown casts.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Acute papillary necrosis (Choice A) occurs following ischemic, inflammatory, infectious, or toxin-mediated damage to the renal papilla and describes the sloughing and loss of the papillae, including substructures such as the distal collecting tubule. It can be triggered by infections (eg, acute pyelonephritis), diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, or NSAIDs. It typically presents with hematuria and acute flank pain.

Atheroembolic renal disease with acute renal infarction (Choice C) can cause acute flank and back pain, nausea, and vomiting. It would typically present with hematuria.

Hypertensive nephrosclerosis (Choice D) can lead to chronic renal failure. Chronic kidney disease is more common in older patients after years of underlying hypertension; it presents with gradually increasing baseline creatinine, as opposed to an abrupt increase followed by normalization or decline.

Volume overload (Choice E), such as in acute or chronic congestive heart failure, can also lead to reduced renal perfusion and acute kidney injury. Volume overload can present with lower extremity edema, pulmonary crackles, and increased jugular venous pressure, none of which are seen in this patient.

questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of progressive shortness of breath that is worse at night. Five days ago, she had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a female newborn at term. Her respirations are 22/min. Bilateral crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Cardiac examination shows the point of maximal impulse to be displaced laterally and an S3 gallop. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia and nonspecific ST-T segment and T-wave changes. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%, global hypokinesis, and mild mitral regurgitation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is a common clinical syndrome encountered in medical practice. Patients typically present with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and lower extremity swelling. Physical examination findings include elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatojugular reflux, pulmonary crackles, and an S3 or S4 gallop. There are many causes of new onset decompensated heart failure, including ischemic heart disease, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, severe valvulopathy, pericardial disease, tachyarrhythmias, and infections. Initial workup should focus on evaluating for these causes with routine laboratory studies, cardiac biomarkers, ECG, chest x-ray, and echocardiography. An ejection fraction less than 50% is considered reduced. This patient presents with orthopnea, pulmonary crackles, displaced point of maximal impulse, an S3 gallop, and echocardiographic evidence of global cardiac dysfunction. Given that this patient recently delivered a healthy, full-term newborn, postpartum cardiomyopathy is the most likely cause of her symptoms. Postpartum cardiomyopathy most commonly develops between 36 weeks’ gestation and up to 1 month after delivery. Risk factors for development include increased age, hypertension during pregnancy, and multiple gestations. Many patients later recover cardiac function but may require ongoing medical management for persistent dysfunction.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E

Coronary artery disease (Choice B) may be associated with ischemic cardiomyopathy. Although it is often asymptomatic, coronary artery disease may cause anginal symptoms or lead to an acute coronary syndrome. Acute coronary syndromes classically present with chest pain radiating to the shoulder or jaw, associated with dyspnea, nausea, and diaphoresis. Prolonged cardiac ischemia from coronary artery disease can lead to ischemic cardiomyopathy and decompensated heart failure. However, this patient has no risk factors for the development of coronary artery disease and no history of cardiac events, making ischemic cardiomyopathy less likely.
Hypertensive heart disease (Choice C) can result in decompensated heart failure. It more commonly causes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and impaired diastolic function due to hypertrophy of the ventricle. However, this requires long-standing high blood pressure and would be unlikely in this young, otherwise healthy patient.

Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) classically presents with acute onset shortness of breath, chest pain, and tachycardia, often in combination with signs of a lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, such as edema or erythema. Large pulmonary emboli can cause cardiac dysfunction, although this dysfunction is more commonly right-sided than global. Thus, despite pregnant women being at higher risk for thrombotic complications, pulmonary embolism is less likely than cardiomyopathy.

Valvular heart disease (Choice E) can cause decompensated heart failure if severe or acute. Commonly, clinically significant valvular disease can be auscultated on physical examination. It will be evident on echocardiography. This patient only has mild mitral regurgitation, making this an unlikely cause of her symptoms.

Educational Objective: Postpartum cardiomyopathy presents after 36 weeks’ gestation and up to 1 month after delivery. It most commonly presents with the symptoms and signs of decompensated heart failure, such as progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, lower extremity swelling, peripheral edema, pulmonary crackles, and an S3 gallop. Evaluation should include routine laboratory studies, cardiac biomarkers, ECG, chest x-ray, and echocardiography with an ejection fraction less than 50% considered reduced. Many patients recover cardiac function but may require ongoing medical management for persistent dysfunction.

questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman who has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 10 years delivers a plethoric, large newborn weighing 5 kg (11 lb). Eighteen hours after delivery, the newborn develops hypoglycemia. Which of the following is the best explanation for the hypoglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: A.  Glucagon secretion by pancreatic α cells is decreased in the newborn

options.label: B
options.html: B.  Hepatic enzymes for gluconeogenesis are increased in the newborn

options.label: C
options.html: C.  Hepatic glycogen content is depleted in the newborn

options.label: D
options.html: D.  Insulin secretion by pancreatic β cells is increased in the newborn

options.label: E
options.html: E.  Maternal insulin crossed the placenta

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Excessive fetal exposure to glucose and insulin in utero can cause macrosomia, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome or hyaline membrane disease, and hypoglycemia in the newborn. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance. This leads to increased concentrations of glucose in the maternal circulation, especially in those with pre-existing diabetes mellitus, and subsequently, the fetal circulation. Fetal hyperglycemia in turn causes the fetus to produce excess insulin, as well as decrease the rate of gluconeogenesis. The insulin then acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia, as in this patient, and inhibits the production of surfactant, which can lead to respiratory distress syndrome. After birth, the fetus continues to synthesize insulin and secrete insulin from the pancreatic β cells at a basal level appropriate for in utero glucose concentrations but is no longer exposed to maternal blood glucose, which leads to hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia presents in the newborn with tremors, diaphoresis, irritability, lethargy, and seizures. Treatment is supportive and includes administration of supplemental glucose while neonatal endocrine regulation self-corrects. Other neonatal complications of maternal diabetes mellitus, which is usually diagnosed by a routine glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks’ gestation, include congenital cardiac and neurologic abnormalities (eg, patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, caudal regression), preterm delivery, polycythemia, and hyperbilirubinemia.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Glucagon secretion by pancreatic α cells is decreased in the newborn (Choice A) is not the primary mediator of neonatal hypoglycemia. While it may be somewhat decreased in utero due to excessive concentrations of glucose, it should return to normal concentrations after birth. Decreased glucagon is not responsible for this patient’s hypoglycemia.

Hepatic enzymes for gluconeogenesis are increased in the newborn (Choice B) is incorrect, as they are decreased after being exposed to excessive glucose and insulin while in utero. These return to normal function in the immediate peripartum period. However, increased gluconeogenesis would result in hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia.

Hepatic glycogen content is depleted in the newborn (Choice C) is not the cause of neonatal hypoglycemia. Infants that have been exposed to significant in utero glucose and insulin have adequate stores of glycogen.

Maternal insulin crossed the placenta (Choice E) is incorrect. Maternal insulin is too large to pass through the placental vessels. Rather, the increased glucose passes through and causes the fetus to create excess insulin, production of which continues after birth. This excessive insulin created by the fetus, rather than transferred from the mother, leads to neonatal hypoglycemia.

Educational Objective: Excessive fetal exposure to glucose and insulin in utero can cause macrosomia, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome or hyaline membrane disease, and hypoglycemia in the newborn. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance. Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which in turn causes the fetus to produce excess insulin, as well as decrease the rate of gluconeogenesis. After birth, the newborn continues to synthesize insulin and secrete insulin from the pancreatic β cells but is no longer exposed to maternal blood glucose, which leads to hypoglycemia.

During transport to the hospital, the newborn develops respiratory distress. The lower ribs and sternum retract on inspiration, and an expiratory grunt is audible. An x-ray of the chest shows uniform reticulogranular densities in both lung fields. Arterial Po2 is 60 mm Hg. Blood and sputum cultures are negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypoxemia in this newborn?

options.label: D

questions.explanationHtml:

questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has the onset of fever, chills, and lower abdominal pain on the second day of her menstrual period. Examination shows tenderness localized to the fallopian tubes and ovaries. A complete blood count shows leukocytosis. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted gram-negative diplococcus that can present with vaginitis, cervicitis, urethritis, disseminated gonorrhea, septic arthritis, or pelvic inflammatory disease. When causing vaginitis, N. gonorrhoeae typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus, although patients may be asymptomatic. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge, as well as an erythematous, friable cervix with cervical motion tenderness. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, it can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which is characterized by cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic signs such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias. Laboratory studies may also show leukocytosis. Complications include tubo-ovarian or intra-abdominal abscess. Diagnosis is made with a nucleic acid amplification test, and treatment is with ceftriaxone.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Gardnerella vaginalis (Choice A) is the organism responsible for bacterial vaginosis, which is a common gynecologic condition characterized by a shift in normal vaginal flora. It presents with gray, thin, malodorous vaginal discharge, a vaginal pH greater than 4.5, a fish-like odor on KOH testing, and clue cells on wet mount preparation. It does not commonly cause leukocytosis or adnexal tenderness.

Staphylococcus aureus (Choice C) is the bacteria most commonly identified in toxic shock syndrome. It produces an exotoxin that causes fever, a diffuse erythematous macular rash, hypotension/distributive shock, and multiorgan system failure. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with gonorrhea.

Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) (Choice D) commonly colonizes the vagina. It is frequently asymptomatic. When found in pregnant patients, it can be a cause of neonatal sepsis after birth, prompting treatment with prophylactic antibiotics during the delivery period. Gonorrhea is the more likely cause of this patient’s symptoms.

Trichomonas vaginalis (Choice E) is an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan that causes vaginal trichomoniasis, which presents with pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia, cervical erythema, and abnormal discharge that is described as green, frothy, and malodorous. Vaginal pH is often greater than 4.5, and motile trichomonads can be seen on wet mount preparation. It does not often progress to cause adnexal tenderness or leukocytosis.

questions.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of vague lower abdominal discomfort. He has been treated with chemotherapy for the last 4 months for testicular embryonal carcinoma. His serum α-fetoprotein concentration, which was initially markedly increased, is now zero. Imaging studies show a persistent 6-cm, well-circumscribed, retroperitoneal mass. The mass is resected and a representative section is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Testicular germ cell tumors account for the majority of testicular carcinoma. Among the germ cell tumors, seminoma occurs most frequently, while nonseminomatous germ cell tumors are classified as either pure or mixed. Histologic patterns include embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, and yolk cell tumor. Mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumors display these histologic types in combination. Embryonal carcinoma is distinguished histologically by poorly differentiated cells with pleomorphic, high-grade nuclear features and displaying solid, glandular, or papillary arrangements. Embryonal carcinomas secrete α-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin. In contrast, teratomas display a variety of differentiated cell types from different germ layers and often display organoid morphology with variable degrees of cellular atypia. Teratomas typically do not secrete either α-fetoprotein or human chorionic gonadotropin. This patient’s photomicrograph shows a biopsy specimen with features of both glandular tissue and cartilage, which would arise from two separate germ layers (eg, endoderm, mesoderm) consistent with a teratoma. Testicular cancers frequently metastasize to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes, which are in the retroperitoneal space. This patient’s biopsy specimen showing glandular and cartilaginous elements is diagnostic of metastatic teratoma and suggests that his primary testicular tumor was of a mixed type, rather than a pure embryonic carcinoma. Treatment includes complete surgical excision and systemic chemotherapy.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Choice A) is incorrect. Retroperitoneal fibrosis is characterized by a fibrotic lesion that typically surrounds the aorta and common iliac artery. It may occur secondary to infection, malignancies, radiation, or drugs, but may occur idiopathically. Histology shows fibrous tissue and chronic inflammation. Cartilaginous tissue is not present.

Metastatic choriocarcinoma (Choice B) is incorrect. Choriocarcinoma is characterized histologically by the presence of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast elements. Choriocarcinoma does not contain elements of cartilage or bone.

Metastatic embryonal carcinoma (Choice C) is incorrect. While this patient was initially diagnosed with embryonal carcinoma, the biopsy specimen showing cartilaginous cells confirms the presence of a teratoma and suggests that the primary testicular carcinoma was of a mixed type.

Scar following chemotherapy (Choice E) is incorrect. Scar tissue does not contain cartilaginous elements and would not be expected to form a large, retroperitoneal mass because of chemotherapy.

Educational Objective: Testicular germ cell tumors account for the majority of testicular carcinoma. Germ cell tumors may be seminomatous or nonseminomatous, and nonseminomatous lesions are frequently of a mixed type, displaying combinations of histopathologic cell types. Teratomas classically display differentiated cell types from more than one germ layer, and often display organoid morphology with variable degrees of cellular atypia.

questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man is diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer. The most appropriate treatment should include a drug with which of the following mechanisms of action?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Prostate cancer is a hormonally sensitive neoplasm, and androgens play a critical role in its growth. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) acts as an agonist of the GnRH receptor and promotes secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) when secreted in its physiologic, pulsatile fashion from the hypothalamus. However, continuous, exogenous administration of a GnRH agonist serves to desensitize the GnRH receptor, thereby decreasing FSH and LH secretion, the stimulation of Leydig cells, and secretion of testosterone. Leuprolide is a GnRH analog that inhibits testosterone production, which reduces the growth of testosterone-sensitive prostate tumors. This hormonal approach to treating prostate cancer is termed medical castration. Some tumors may become castration-resistant, in which mutations develop that allow the cancer to continue growing without hormonal stimulation. Hormonal therapy can be used in combination with surgical excision, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Androstenedione aromatase inhibitors (Choice A), such as exemestane, irreversibly inhibit production of estrone and estradiol, which is useful for treatment of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. Other aromatase inhibitors, such as the nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor anastrazole, inhibit aromatase through competitive inhibition.

Estrogen receptor partial agonist-antagonist (Choice B) behavior characterizes the mechanism of action of selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), such as tamoxifen. Tamoxifen is useful for the management of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer but plays no role in the management of prostate cancer.

Microtubule function inhibition (Choice D) is the mechanism of action of a variety of chemotherapeutic agents, such as taxanes (eg, paclitaxel and docetaxel) and vinca alkaloids (eg, vincristine and vinblastine). Taxanes are second-line chemotherapeutic agents for prostate cancer and are typically reserved for castration-resistant tumors.

Somatostatin receptor agonists (Choice E), such as octreotide, are useful for the management of carcinoid tumors and VIPoma (tumors that secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide). They are not useful for the management of prostate cancer.

Educational Objective: Leuprolide, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist, is used in prostate cancer as a form of medical castration. Continuous administration of leuprolide decreases luteinizing hormone release by the pituitary gland and subsequently decreases the production of testosterone by the Leydig cells.

questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man comes to the physician with his 27-year-old wife because they have been unable to conceive for 1 year. Previous examination of the wife showed no abnormalities. Physical examination shows normal genitalia. His serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone concentrations are within the reference ranges and serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is increased. Semen analysis shows decreased sperm count. A decreased serum concentration of which of following is the most likely in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Sertoli-cell­–only syndrome, also known as germinal cell aplasia, is a rare disorder in which only Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, indicating an absence of germ cells and spermatogonia with resultant failure in spermatogenesis. The cause is not completely understood but is thought to have an underlying genetic cause in at least some cases. Under normal conditions, the seminiferous tubules are lined by spermatogonia, which generate the primary spermatocytes that will ultimately become sperm. Sertoli cells are also present within the seminiferous tubules and are required to support spermatogenesis. Pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone produced by the hypothalamus causes the pituitary gland to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). LH acts on the Leydig cells, located adjacent to the seminiferous tubules, and causes them to secrete testosterone. FSH acts on the Sertoli cells, leading them to produce androgen-binding protein and promote sperm development. Additionally, Sertoli cells provide negative feedback on hypothalamic FSH secretion by producing inhibin B. Inhibin B concentration correlates directly with sperm count and is typically decreased or undetectable in patients with Sertoli-cell–only syndrome. The diagnosis of Sertoli-cell–only syndrome is suggested by normal testosterone and LH concentrations, increased FSH concentration, and azoospermia (lack of sperm) on semen analysis, although testicular biopsy is required to confirm the absence of germ cells.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Androstenedione (Choice A) is a precursor of testosterone. It is converted to testosterone by 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase within Leydig cells. Most patients with Sertoli-cell–only syndrome have normal concentrations of testosterone and androstenedione.

Dihydrotestosterone (Choice B) is an androgenic hormone that is produced from testosterone by Δ4-5α–dehydrogenase. While it plays an important role in sexual differentiation and development of secondary sexual characteristics, it does not play an important role in spermatogenesis and is typically normal in patients with Sertoli-cell–only syndrome.

Estradiol (Choice C) is produced by Leydig cells. While estradiol does play a role in spermatogenesis by regulating spermatogonia proliferation and differentiation, defective estradiol production does not underlie Sertoli-cell–only syndrome.

Sex hormone-binding globulin (Choice E) is a hepatically produced serum protein that carries circulating testosterone and estradiol. Its concentration is not affected by defects in spermatogenesis.

Educational Objective: Sertoli-cell–only syndrome is a rare disorder in which only Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, indicating an absence of germ cells and spermatogonia with resultant failure in spermatogenesis. Patients exhibit abnormally reduced inhibin B production by Sertoli cells due to the absence of spermatogonia. The diagnosis of Sertoli-cell–only syndrome is suggested by normal testosterone and luteinizing hormone concentrations, increased follicle-stimulating hormone concentration, and azoospermia (lack of sperm) on semen analysis, although testicular biopsy is required to confirm the absence of germ cells.

questions.stemHtml: 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of palpitations; she also has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this period. Her pulse is 110/min. Physical examination shows a goiter and a fine resting tremor. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of <0.1 μU/mL and thyroxine (T4 ) concentration of 50 μg/dL. A thyroidal iodine (123 I) uptake scan is shown. Which of the following structures is identified by the arrow in this image?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

This patient presents with hyperthyroidism, as evidenced by findings of weight loss, tremor, palpitations, reduced serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration, and increased serum thyroxine (T4)  concentration. Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism and is caused by an autoantibody that stimulates the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells. Excessive stimulation of the TSH receptor leads to follicular thyroid hyperplasia and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. Serum laboratory studies may show increased concentrations of triiodothyronine (T3) and T4, decreased TSH, and the presence of TSH receptor stimulating antibodies. Nuclear medicine studies may be performed with iodine-123 or technetium 99m pertechnetate and will generally show diffuse, homogenously increased thyroid activity, as in this patient. While most patients with or without hyperthyroidism have a bilobed thyroid gland, a minority possess a third lobe known as a pyramidal lobe. The pyramidal lobe is a remnant of the thyroglossal duct and is usually located at the isthmus of the thyroid gland, extending superiorly toward the hyoid bone. The presence of a pyramidal lobe is considered a normal anatomic variant of the thyroid gland.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Ectopic thyroid tissue (Choice A) is incorrect. While ectopic thyroid tissue may exist at any point along the course of the thyroglossal duct, the tissue observed in this patient is connected to the thyroid gland near the isthmus and likely represents a pyramidal lobe.

Parathyroid gland (Choice B) is incorrect. The parathyroid glands are located on the posterior aspects of the two lobes of the thyroid gland. Parathyroid tissue does not take up iodine-123 and is not typically visible on nuclear medicine studies, except with scans using technetium 99m sestamibi.

Salivary gland tumor (Choice D) is incorrect. While salivary gland tumors may rarely present in the thyroid gland, where they may mimic thyroid carcinoma, they do not absorb iodine-123 on nuclear medicine studies.

Thyroid adenoma (Choice E) is incorrect. Thyroid adenomas may display variable patterns of iodine-123 uptake. This patient’s scan shows diffusely and homogenously increased uptake within both thyroid lobes as well as the indicated structure, which is less consistent with an adenoma.

questions.stemHtml: An 18-year-old woman with a 3-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of light-headedness and urinary frequency with a large volume of urine. She has had nausea and has not eaten or taken her insulin for the past 2 days. She appears tired. Her pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 98/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. Her breath has a fruity aroma. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely occurring in this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: B.  Decreased gluconeogenesis from lactic acid

options.label: D
options.html: D.  Increased activity of hormone-sensitive lipase

options.label: F
options.html: F.   Increased glycogen synthesis in the liver

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs as a result of accumulation of serum ketones such as β-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of insulin deficiency, and is more common in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Patients present with signs and symptoms of tachycardia, tachypnea, fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Laboratory studies typically show increased serum glucose and ketones, metabolic acidosis, and a high anion gap caused by the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. Absent insulin signaling leads to DKA by causing a perceived energy deficient state, causing dysregulated secretion of glucagon and upregulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis. Ketone bodies provide an alternate source of energy in the absence of insulin-mediated delivery of glucose. The production of ketone bodies in DKA is regulated in part by hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL). HSL is expressed in adipose tissue, where it hydrolyzes fatty acids from triacylglycerols or diacylglycerols. HSL is stimulated by catecholamines and inhibited by insulin. The absence of insulin in DKA leads to increased HSL-mediated lipolysis. Free fatty acids are then made available for hepatic beta oxidation, producing acetyl coenzyme A, which is in turn used to synthesize ketone bodies during hepatic ketogenesis. DKA is treated with replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions.

Decreased formation of 3-hydroxybutyric acid (Choice A) would not be observed. 3-hydroxybutyric acid is formed in increased amounts in patients with DKA.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of episodes of fainting during the past 2 weeks. She also has a 3-month history of easy fatigability, irritability, headaches on awakening, and extreme hunger. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Her serum glucose concentration is 35 mg/dL. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a mass in the pancreas. Immunohistochemical labeling of neoplastic cells obtained on biopsy of the mass is most likely to involve the use of antibodies directed to which of the following pancreatic secretory products?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Insulinoma is a rare neoplasm of pancreatic islet cells that functionally produces insulin. These neoplastic cells classically do not respond to typical feedback mechanisms, and as a result, insulin is continuously produced even in periods of hypoglycemia. Patients present with symptoms of hypoglycemia, which are generally neuroglycopenic (agitation, headache, blurry vision, diplopia, tremor), autonomic (diaphoresis, tremoring, nausea, vomiting, cramping, tachycardia, anxiety), and nonspecific (fatigue, weakness, lethargy), often exacerbated by periods of fasting or exercise. In extreme cases, hypoglycemia can present with seizures, coma, arrhythmias, and death. Whipple triad characterizes the presentation of hypoglycemia in the setting of likely insulinoma or excess insulin, and includes 1) signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, 2) concomitant serum glucose less than 45 mg/dL, and 3) reversibility of symptoms with administration of glucose. Insulinomas seldom metastasize and are considered predominantly benign neuroendocrine tumors apart from their dysregulated functional production of hormone. They are occasionally associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia. Diagnosis of an insulinoma is via laboratory studies showing increased serum proinsulin, insulin, and C peptide, and decreased glucose, along with CT scan or MRI of the pancreas. Definitive treatment requires surgical resection.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Gastrin (Choice A) is produced by gastrinomas, which are associated with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Gastrinomas result in excessive production of acid by the gastric parietal cells. This can lead to recurrent, chronic duodenal or jejunal ulcers, which can present with abdominal pain, diarrhea secondary to malabsorption, and possible hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia.

Glucagon (Choice B) is produced by glucagonomas, a rare pancreatic tumor. Excessive glucagon production raises blood glucose. Symptoms are nonspecific and include mild diabetes mellitus, paraneoplastic rash (eg, necrolytic migratory erythema), and weight loss.

Somatostatin (Choice D) is produced by somatostatinomas. Somatostatinomas are an uncommon neuroendocrine malignancy that presents with weight loss, mild diabetes mellitus, steatorrhea as a result of limited cholecystokinin release, and achlorhydria from inhibition of gastrin.

Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) (Choice E) is produced by a vipoma. Vipoma is a rare tumor often associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia. Patients present with chronic and profound watery diarrhea, electrolyte disturbances (eg, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia), achlorhydria, alkalosis, flushing, vasodilation, and hypercalcemia. This syndrome is often termed WDHA syndrome (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria).

questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman has been hospitalized for 2 weeks because of severe pneumonia complicated by septicemia and respiratory failure. She has a long-standing history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and a family history of chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis. Her serum triiodothyronine (T3 ) and thyroxine (T4 ) concentrations are below the reference ranges, and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 concentrations are within the reference ranges. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: D
options.html: D.  Increased serum T4 -binding globulin concentration

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Euthyroid sick syndrome describes abnormalities in thyroid function testing that occur in the setting of acute systemic illness. Euthyroid sick syndrome has been observed in the setting of brain injury, myocardial infarction, pneumonia, cirrhosis, end-stage kidney disease, diabetic ketoacidosis, starvation, malignancy, and following trauma or major surgery. The cause of this syndrome is not completely understood, but it is hypothesized that critical illness and acute phase, proinflammatory cytokines alter normal thyroid signaling in a variety of mechanisms, such as downregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis at the level of the hypothalamus, by altering the action of deiodinases and thyroid binding globulin, and by altering expression and function of thyroid receptors. The most frequently observed findings are decreased serum concentration of free triiodothyronine (T3), normal or low thyroxine (T4) and free T4, and a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration. Patients are clinically euthyroid and do not display overt clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism. Treatment targets the underlying illness, and abnormalities in laboratory studies generally resolve with resolution of the primary disease.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Antithyroid antibodies (Choice A) are characteristic of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, also known as Hashimoto disease. Patients present with signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism caused by destruction of thyroid parenchyma.

Hypothyroidism (Choice C) can occur as a result of hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis dysfunction, primary thyroid dysfunction, or autoimmune disease, and presents with signs and symptoms such as weight gain, lethargy, fatigue, constipation, hair loss, and cold intolerance. The presence of abnormal thyroid function testing and lack of overt symptoms of hypothyroidism in the context of acute illness suggests euthyroid sick syndrome.

Increased serum T4-binding globulin concentration (Choice D) may occur in patients with hypothyroidism and is often secondary to hormonal disturbances associated with pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and liver dysfunction.

Iodine deficiency (Choice E) is incorrect. Thyroid follicular iodine stores are sufficient to support thyroid function for several months. Iodine deficiency is rare in the developed world due to fortification of common food staples with iodine.

The most frequently observed findings are decreased serum concentration of free triiodothyronine (T3), normal or low thyroxine (T4) and free T4, and a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration. Patients are clinically euthyroid and do not display overt clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-week history of a rash on her face and hands; the rash is exacerbated by sun exposure. She also has had difficulty climbing stairs and holding her arms above her head, such as when combing her hair. Examination of the hands shows the findings in the photograph. This patient most likely has which of the following underlying conditions?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Cancer, especially adenocarcinomas such as ovarian cancer, are associated with dermatomyositis as a paraneoplastic syndrome. Dermatomyositis presents with cutaneous and musculoskeletal manifestations. Cutaneous manifestations include pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope rash), pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), and light pink to lilac-colored patches with telangiectasias over the upper back and sun-exposed chest (poikilodermatous rash). Musculoskeletal findings include proximal muscle weakness of the extremities. Diagnosis is made with a combination of clinical findings and serologic testing, including antinuclear antibody, anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2 antibodies. Patients diagnosed with dermatomyositis should undergo further workup including age-appropriate cancer screening to rule out underlying occult malignancy.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Amyloidosis (Choice A) results from deposition of amyloid that may be genetic or acquired secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions or lymphoproliferative malignancy. Diagnosis is based on histopathologic examination of tissue from affected organs stained with Congo red showing green birefringent crystals under polarized light.

Bronchiectasis (Choice B) is abnormal dilatation of the bronchi that may result from recurrent necrotizing infections and chronic inflammation. Risk factors for bronchiectasis include cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

Optic artery occlusion (Choice D) commonly results from an embolic source as in carotid artery stenosis or from valvular vegetations of endocarditis. Skin findings associated with endocarditis include splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, and Janeway lesions. It presents with sudden, painless vision loss.

Renal failure (Choice E) is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Acute SLE is associated with cutaneous findings including malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds and erythema of the skin over the dorsal digits between the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. Systemic complications of acute SLE include arthralgias, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypercoagulability, and lupus nephritis, which is a common cause of renal failure in young patients. Diagnosis of SLE is based on serologic and clinical findings.

Cutaneous findings include a heliotrope rash involving the periocular area, Gottron papules overlying the joints of the dorsal hands, and a poikilodermatous rash in a shawl distribution. Patients are diagnosed with dermatomyositis based on clinical and serologic findings, including the presence of autoantibodies. questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 45-minute history of abdominal pain, diaphoresis, and weakness. Two hours ago, he spilled a chemical on his left arm while mixing the solution for crop dusting. His respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 100/55 mm Hg. Physical examination shows salivation, wheezing, diaphoresis, and muscle weakness. After confirming the identity of the solution, the physician begins treatment with atropine and pralidoxime. The chemical solution most likely contained which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Anticholinesterase poisoning is caused by the irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase (AChE), which is an enzyme that acts to degrade acetylcholine (ACh). ACh acts on both nicotinic and muscarinic ACh receptors. Nicotinic ACh receptors are found in autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, and skeletal muscle, whereas muscarinic ACh receptors are found in the heart, brain, smooth muscle, exocrine glands, and sweat glands. Inhibitors of AChE inhibit ACh degradation and lead to excess levels of ACh in the neuromuscular junction. This can result in vomiting, diarrhea, urination, diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, seizures, and muscle weakness. A common cause of anticholinesterase poisoning includes organophosphates, which are commonly found in insecticides. Exposure can occur transcutaneously, or via inhalation or ingestion. Triggering agents found in organophosphates include parathion, fenthion, and malathion, among others. Treatment involves decontamination along with atropine to antagonize the muscarinic receptors and pralidoxime to regenerate functional AChE.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Carbaryl (Choice A) is a chemical used in insecticides. It is also a cholinesterase inhibitor that can lead to toxicity in humans through ingestion, inhalation, or dermal absorption. It typically causes less severe symptoms for shorter periods of time, as it only transiently inhibits AChE before spontaneously dissociating.

2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (Choice B) is a commonly used herbicide. It is generally not toxic to humans and would not be expected to cause the cholinergic symptoms seen in this patient.

Paraquat (Choice C) is a commonly used herbicide. While it is toxic to humans, ingestion or inhalation are more significant routes of exposure. It would more commonly present with lung injury followed by multiorgan failure. It would not be expected to cause the symptoms seen in this patient.

Pyrethrin (Choice E) is an organic insecticide derived from chrysanthemum flowers. It can cause toxicity in humans when inhaled or when there is prolonged dermal exposure, but, in general, it is not considered particularly harmful.

questions.stemHtml: Public health officials in a large metropolitan city in the US would like to decrease the prevalence of obesity in the city’s population. A tax on carbonated and other sugar-based beverages is subsequently implemented. Which of the following best describes this type of intervention?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

A tax on carbonated and sugar-based beverages is an example of a community intervention strategy. Community intervention strategies define the setting for and target of intervention as the community, as opposed to interventions aimed toward an individual. Such interventions can take place in a variety of settings, such as at the municipal level, through schools, churches, or other organizations. Community interventions aim to improve the health of the population by influencing decision-making throughout the community. For such strategies to succeed, they require knowledge of the community, its health and socioeconomic challenges, and identification of appropriate points of intervention.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, and D.

Clinical intervention (Choice A) describes intervention strategies that take place in a clinical setting. Clinical interventions may employ primary, secondary, or tertiary strategies by preventing, identifying, and treating disease.

Secondary intervention (Choice C) strategies employ screening to identify individuals with disease early in their course, generally while remaining subclinical. A secondary intervention strategy would be to screen an obese population for hypertension or diabetes, detecting disease before symptoms or consequences have arisen.

Tertiary intervention (Choice D) strategies aim to slow or ameliorate the progression and complications of a disease through therapeutic intervention. An example would be to treat an obese patient with known diabetes to prevent further macrovascular complications.

questions.stemHtml: A study of 10 patients with severe emphysema who were treated with oral theophylline for 12 weeks found no improvement in the exercise ability of these patients after treatment. Which of the following best describes this study design?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

A case series study is a descriptive study that describes the history, possible exposures, clinical findings, and treatment results of a group of patients with a similar diagnosis. Case series are non-analytic studies and do not imply a cause-and-effect relationship. They do not test a hypothesis nor are they randomized. They are useful in characterizing the natural history of a disease or response to treatment and are also useful for evaluating the outcomes of a particular procedure or patient population at a single institution. They are useful in describing rare diseases, as the small population size may not permit conduction of a larger cohort, or randomized trials with sufficient power.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Case-control studies (Choice B) investigate an association between an exposure and an outcome. In this study design, a group of patients with the disease (cases) are identified. A group of patients without the disease (controls) are matched on baseline characteristics to the cases. Exposure data for the two groups is collected, and these data are compared to determine association with the outcome (disease) in question. An odds ratio may be calculated to compare exposures between groups.

Cohort studies (Choice C) identify a group of patients with or without an exposure and follow them over time to identify whether an exposure is associated with an outcome of interest. Cohort studies may be retrospective or prospective in design. In a prospective design, the hypothesis and analysis protocols are established prior to the start of the study period. In a retrospective design, the hypothesis or question is designed after the study time period has passed.

A randomized controlled trial (Choice D) is an experimental study design. Patients are randomly allocated to two or more interventional or control arms, and these patients are followed over time to evaluate an outcome of interest. Randomized design minimizes opportunity for bias; thus, a randomized interventional study can be used to imply causation. Common examples of randomized trials include therapeutic comparisons between a new drug and the previous standard of care.

A systematic review (Choice E) is a study design in which ideally all known studies pertaining to a particular topic are collected according to a predetermined set of criteria. Systematic reviews typically include meta-analysis, in which statistical analysis is performed to combine the results of multiple studies addressing the same question. Systematic review and meta-analysis are useful for overcoming certain (importantly, not all) limitations of the constituent studies. By pooling the results of multiple studies, this method reduces the risk for Type II error caused by the smaller sample sizes within each constituent study. On the converse, methodologic error from individual studies still influences the result of the systematic review and meta-analysis.

Educational Objective: A case series is a descriptive study that describes the history, possible exposures, clinical findings, and treatment results of a group of patients with a similar diagnosis. Case series studies are useful for studying the outcomes or natural history of a particular group, procedure, or treatment.

In a retrospective design, the hypothesis or question is designed after the study period has passed. In this study, patients are observed over time and divided into groups based on use of oral contraceptives or tubal ligation (exposure) and are followed over time. Rates of cervical cancer (outcome) are compared between the two groups. The relative risk for cervical cancer (a comparison of incidence) is then calculated to be six times as high in the oral contraceptive group. This represents a prospective cohort study design.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after fainting while at work. He is conscious and is able to state his name and what he was doing before the episode. He says that he has had fatigue during the past 3 weeks. He has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. His mother died of ovarian cancer at the age of 40 years. His maternal grandfather died of colon cancer at the age of 49 years. The patient does not smoke or drink alcoholic beverages. He appears pale. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 6.2 g/dL and hematocrit of 19%. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Colonoscopy shows an isolated right-sided mass. Examination of a biopsy specimen of the mass shows a poorly-differentiated adenocarcinoma with mucinous features. Immunohistochemistry of the biopsy specimen is most likely to show loss of expression of which of the following proteins?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a high risk for colorectal cancer (CRC), along with endometrial, ovarian, gastric, hepatobiliary, pancreas, brain, and skin cancer. It is caused by defects in DNA mismatch repair genes, including MSH2, MSH6, and MLH1, which have a key role in correcting DNA replication errors. These proteins remove mismatched nucleotides from newly synthesized single DNA strands. The resulting gaps are filled in using the parent strand as a template. Dysfunction of mismatch repair proteins increases the frequency of spontaneous mutations and causes high microsatellite instability, increasing the risk for cancer. Lynch syndrome comprises 2% to 5% of all cases of CRC, but 80% of patients with Lynch syndrome develop CRC, typically at a younger age than in sporadic cases. Patients with a family history suspicious for a cancer syndrome should undergo genetic counseling; microsatellite instability profiling and immunohistochemistry testing for mismatch repair gene expression are the gold standard to confirm diagnosis. Patients with Lynch syndrome should undergo CRC screening with colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years beginning at age 25, or 5 years before the first age of diagnosis in the family, and then annually beginning at age 35. Alternatively, patients can undergo prophylactic colectomy, along with prophylactic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in biologically female patients.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

APC (Choice A) is a tumor suppressor gene that regulates cellular proliferation and cell adhesion. Inactivating mutations are implicated in most sporadic cases of CRC as the first step in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, a pathway of sporadic mutations that promotes progression to cancer. Germline mutations in APC are the cause of familial adenomatous polyposis, characterized by the development of thousands of colonic polyps and a 100% lifetime risk for development of CRC.

BRCA1 (Choice B) is a tumor suppressor gene involved in DNA double-strand break repair. Inherited germline mutations of BRCA1 are associated with an increased risk for breast cancer, including male breast cancer, along with ovarian, gastric, pancreatic, prostate, and colon cancer. Cancer risk can be decreased with prophylactic mastectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

β-Catenin (Choice C) is a proto-oncogene that regulates cell to cell adhesion and gene transcription. Sporadic mutations are implicated in a wide range of cancers including colorectal, ovarian, breast, lung, brain, and liver cancer. However, a familial cancer syndrome caused by a germline mutation in β-catenin has not been described, and this gene is not one of the adenoma-carcinoma sequence genes commonly found in sporadic cases of CRC.

p53 (Choice E) is a tumor suppressor that limits oncogene transcription and promotes transcription of genes that inhibit cell division. Dysfunctional or inactivating mutations of p53 are a common finding in many solid tumors, including as a late step in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of sporadic CRC. Germline mutations in p53 are the cause of Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by high risk for sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia, and adrenal gland cancer.

Educational Objective: Inherited defects in DNA mismatch repair genes are the cause of Lynch syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a high risk for colorectal cancer, along with endometrial, ovarian, gastric, hepatobiliary, pancreas, brain, and skin cancer. Patients with Lynch syndrome should undergo screening colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years beginning at age 25, or 5 years before the first age of diagnosis in the family, and then annually beginning at age 35. Additional treatment options include prophylactic colectomy, hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

questions.stemHtml: A study is conducted to assess the normal frequency distribution of plasma sodium concentrations in a given population. Results show that the mean is 141 mEq/L and the standard deviation is 3.2 mEq/L. Which of the following best represents the percentage of values that will fall in the interval between 134.6 mEq/L and 147.4 mEq/L?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

In a Gaussian (normal) distribution, data points center around the mean value. Standard deviation is a measure of the degree of dispersion of data points about the mean and is defined as the square root of the variance. In a Gaussian distribution, one standard deviation above and below the mean will include approximately 68% of data points, while two standard deviations above and below the mean will include approximately 95% of data points. Three standard deviations above and below the mean will include approximately 99.7% of data points. In a population with a mean sodium of 141 mEq/L and a standard deviation of 3.2 mEq/L, individuals with sodium between 134.6 mEq/L and 147.4 mEq/L will fall within two standard deviations below and above the mean, respectively. Therefore, this range of values will include approximately 95% of the values in this distribution.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, G, and H

25% (Choice A), 50% (Choice C), and 90% (Choice E) do not correspond with a percentage of values within or outside of one, two, or three standard deviations of the mean.

33% (Choice B) roughly corresponds to the total percentage of values found outside of the range of one standard deviation above or below the mean, while 67% (Choice D) roughly corresponds to the percentage of values that lie within one standard deviation from the mean.

97.5% (Choice G) is not correct. Five percent of data points in total lie outside of the range of two standard deviations above and below the mean, with half of these data points (2.5%) above this range and the other half (2.5%) below. Therefore, 97.5% represents the percentage of all values above 134.6 mEq/L (95% within two standard deviations from the mean plus 2.5% above this range) or the percentage of all values below 147.4 mEq/L (95% within two standard deviations from the mean plus 2.5% below this range).

99% (Choice H) roughly corresponds to the percentage of data points found within three standard deviations above and below the mean (99.7%).

Educational Objective: In a normal distribution, standard deviation describes the degree of dispersion of data points about the mean. Sixty-eight percent of data points lie within one standard deviation above and below the mean, 95% of data points lie within two standard deviations above and below the mean, and 99.7% of data points lie within three standard deviations above and below the mean.

questions.stemHtml: Numerous cross-sectional studies in different populations have shown a significant relationship between the use of tanning beds and the development of melanoma. The odds ratios of these studies range from 3.2 to 7.1. In these studies, the number of hours of tanning bed use was highly correlated with an increase in the size and number of dysplastic nevi. Which of the following is the greatest limitation in establishing causality from these studies?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

A cross-sectional study seeks to identify the prevalence of a condition at a particular point in time. In this scenario, these studies examine the use of tanning beds and the development of melanoma at a single cross-section of time. Thus, the risk factor (tanning beds) and the outcomes (melanoma) are measured simultaneously. Cross-sectional studies do not follow patients over time. All information is collected at a single point, so causation cannot be determined because the temporal sequence of events cannot be examined. In these studies, the development of melanoma may have preceded the use of tanning beds. Cross-sectional studies can, however, determine correlation. Correlation relates the trends of two variables together and is quantified by the Pearson correlation coefficient (r). It represents the increase, decrease, or absence, or absence of change in one variable with changes in the other.

In cases where variables trend together (both increase), the r value is positive. The closer the value of the correlation coefficient to 1.0, the stronger the trend between the two variables. Negative r values suggest that data trend in opposing fashion; as one variable increases, the other decreases. Uncorrelated data will have a correlation coefficient near zero, which indicates that changes in one variable are not associated with any trend in the other variable. Correlation should not be confused with causation.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Biologic plausibility (Choice A) is not the correct answer for this choice. Biologic plausibility exists for these studies, as there is well-known evidence that exposure to UV light can lead to skin cancer, such as melanoma.

Consistency of the findings (Choice B) is inaccurate. These studies have consistent findings with highly positive odds ratios in all studies. Despite including numerous studies with consistent findings, causality remains difficult to interpret given the unknown timing of events.

Dose response (Choice C) is present in these studies, as increased hours of tanning was associated with an increased risk for melanoma. This seems to be consistent across studies. An increased dose response favors causality but does not prove it.

Strength of association (Choice D) also favors causality. In these studies, there seems to be a high strength of association with odds ratios ranging from 3.2 to 7.1, indicating a significantly increased risk for melanoma with tanning bed exposure. This would not inhibit the ability to infer causality.

Educational Objective: A cross-sectional study seeks to identify the prevalence of a condition at a particular point in time. Because the risk factor and the outcomes are measured at the same time, the temporal sequence of events cannot be determined. This inhibits the ability to infer causality. Biologic plausibility, consistent findings, a strong dose response, and a strong association increase the likelihood of causality but do not prove it.

questions.stemHtml: An 18-year-old female college freshman comes to the health center because of a 3-month history of fatigue and intermittent headaches. She also has had an unintentional weight loss of 4 kg (9 lb) during the past 6 weeks and difficulty concentrating on her schoolwork. She moved from her home to a campus dormitory 5 months ago. She was an avid tennis player but says she has not played since school began because she has no energy and has lost interest in sports. She notes that she recently broke off her long-distance relationship with her boyfriend back home. She tearfully says she feels lonely and is frustrated with her performance on final examinations. She occasionally drinks alcoholic beverages "to help with sleep." She does not use illicit drugs. She appears thin and has a sad affect. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: A.      "Although this is a difficult time for many, I'm concerned that you're not coping well. Have you had any feelings of hurting yourself?"

options.label: B
options.html: B.       "Have you made any friends on campus yet? Sometimes a student support group is the best remedy for transitional stress."

options.label: C
options.html: C.      "It seems that this difficult transition has made you depressed. What are your thoughts about receiving additional care in the hospital, where you can be in a safe environment?"

options.label: D
options.html: D.     "It's normal to feel homesick and lonely during your first year away from home. Planning a visit home to be with your family might help you feel better."

options.label: E
options.html: E.       "Transitioning to college life is difficult for many students. It will get better once you become accustomed to your surroundings."

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

This young patient is exhibiting neurovegetative symptoms suggestive of major depressive disorder (MDD). The physician should express concern about the patient’s well-being and conduct a thorough suicide risk assessment including questions about suicidal ideation or attempts.

Symptoms of MDD typically include 2 or more weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor slowing, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. Some patients present with vague somatic symptoms such as headaches. Suicide is the most serious and acute risk for patients with MDD, so physicians should ask detailed questions about patients’ suicidal ideation and recent or remote suicide attempts.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Suggesting a support group by stating "Have you made any friends on campus yet? Sometimes a student support group is the best remedy for transitional stress." (Choice B) or encouraging a family visit by stating "It's normal to feel homesick and lonely during your first year away from home. Planning a visit home to be with your family might help you feel better." (Choice D) may be appropriate later in the interview, particularly given that the patient reports loneliness. However, the physician’s first priority should be evaluating the patient’s safety.

Suggesting psychiatric hospitalization (Choice C) may be warranted if the patient reports active suicidal ideation. However, the physician should first assess the patient’s safety.

Reassuring the patient that her transition experience is normal (Choice E) would be inaccurate, as the patient appears to have MDD. Further, the physician’s priority should be evaluating the patient’s safety.

Educational Objective: Major depressive disorder can manifest with vague somatic symptoms in conjunction with decreased energy, increased or decreased sleep, and increased or decreased appetite. Suicide is the most acute and serious risk for major depressive disorder and should be assessed regularly in patients with suspected major depressive disorder.
